#203251. Donkeys help families survive droughts, but governments often overlook them

Donkeys help families survive droughts, but governments often overlook them

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1486 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Donkeys help East African families survive severe droughts, yet governments and aid organizations often overlook their essential needs.
  • Industry observers note that families in East Africa depend on donkeys for many everyday tasks.
  • Industry observers note that in a drought their job gets even more important.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Donkeys help East African families survive severe droughts, yet governments and aid organizations often overlook their essential needs.

Industry observers note that families in East Africa depend on donkeys for many everyday tasks. The animals carry water, feed for livestock, and household belongings. They have also been part of local culture for generations.

Industry observers note that in a drought their job gets even more important. Once the water close to home has dried up, donkeys trek long distances to bring it back.

Industry observers note that yet when drought relief arrives, donkeys are rarely part of it. Aid has tended to go to the food-producing animals, and donkey-owning households end up worse off for it.

A team from the University of Portsmouth, Maasai Mara University and Haramaya University looked at how far that neglect goes.

They went through 77 documents and talked with 41 people on the ground. Donkeys, it turned out, are mostly missing, from the policies right down to the vet schools.

It has been revealed that from 2020 to 2023 East Africa was hit by drought. Crops failed widely and some places lost up to 70% of livestock.

Around 26 million people were threatened with food shortages, and conflict over the dwindling resources went up.

Many of the worst affected families are pastoralists, meaning their living depends on herds that often move with them.

Donkeys have been part of that life since they were domesticated in Africa thousands of years ago.

It has been revealed that when nearby sources dry up, the water a donkey brings back keeps people, crops and herds going. Donkeys also get people to health facilities, aid distribution centers and markets.

Sources indicate that kenya and Ethiopia both rely heavily on them. Ethiopia has about 10.8 million donkeys, and Kenya around 1.2 million.

Professor Leanne Proops works on animal behavior and welfare at the University of Portsmouth and supervised the project.

“Working donkeys are a lifeline for many communities during drought, helping people access water, transport essential supplies and sustain their livelihoods,” stated Proops.

“Yet their contribution is largely overlooked in the policies and support systems designed to help communities cope with these crises.”.

Of the 77 documents, 51 were Kenyan and 26 Ethiopian, issued anywhere from 1964 up to 2025.

Animal health, agriculture, climate change, disaster risk and water were the areas covered. Equids, that is donkeys, horses and mules, came up in just 17.

Quite often the donkey got one mention in a species list and was absent from the rest of the policy.

According to recent reports, “Livestock” was a word used a lot, but most documents never said what species it took in. In reality it meant cattle, sheep and goats.

Donkeys, on the occasions they did appear, sat outside conventional livestock under labels such as “working animals” or “emerging livestock.”.

Not one of the documents made a link between donkeys and drought, even though camels were mentioned in that role.

Recent findings suggest that on welfare the picture is not much better. Kenya’s Animal Welfare and Protection Bill has been in deliberation since 2019 without being enacted.

Up until 2025, Ethiopia’s criminal code only made cruelty an offense when it happened where the public could see.

A 2025 proclamation now prohibits overloading or overworking any working animal, though no penalties are set out in that part.

In a recent development, references to animals in the policies were heavily based on use, with meat, milk, hides and exports driving them. Kenya’s 2024 Livestock Bill does define donkeys as draught animals but welfare hardly features.

It has been revealed that the interviews pointed the same way. If a drought is forecast, preparedness intends kick in with worming and vaccination for the other livestock.

“The donkeys were generally left out. Nobody was thinking about them,” one participant in Kenya told the researchers.

Later on, supplementary feed rations get handed out in both countries and again the donkeys are not counted.

A participant in Ethiopia stated that when fodder runs short, “the priority is not for donkeys, not for mules, just for animals with salvage value.”.

In the only program one Kenyan participant had worked on with donkeys included, they got rabies vaccination and no food. The rest of the animals were counted for supplementary feeding.

Participants also noted that droughts are far more frequent than before. Money often comes towards the end, when much has died.

Pastoralists summed this up in their own words: “money comes with the vultures.”.

Recent findings suggest that dr. Emily Haddy, lead author of the paper, did the work at Portsmouth and is now at the University of Nottingham.

“Recognising donkeys in livestock and disaster planning is not just an animal welfare matter,” said Haddy.

“By including working donkeys in drought preparedness and emergency responses, governments and aid organisations can help protect animal welfare and strengthen community resilience.”.

In a recent development, the veterinarians taking part spoke of getting little or no training on donkeys. One participant in Kenya noted they try to extrapolate from horses, which does not always hold.

“We try to extrapolate what we know from the horse to the donkey, which is not always true,” the participant stated.

Vets specializing in donkeys are few and tend to be in urban areas such as Nairobi. Pastoralist communities therefore often have no access, and lose animals that could have been treated.

Medications suitable for donkeys are also in short supply, particularly anesthesia and pain relief.

“I don’t even think there is any organization in Kenya which makes feeds for donkeys,” another participant said.

According to recent reports, it should be noted the vets interviewed were older graduates. Donkey medicine in the Kenyan vet curriculum has recently improved, though its effect on the ground may take time.

According to participants, the priority for government is animals bringing in foreign currency directly, through sale of meat and hides.

According to recent reports, the services of a donkey are largely invisible. That makes them hard to quantify and keeps them out of national economic reports.

It has been revealed that one participant described a child-focused relief scheme for milk. Donkeys play a vital role in that milk chain, but they were not taken into account.

“They see the human being first, and they see the cattle, the producer of the milk, and the consumer of the milk, the in-between connection they don’t see,” the participant said.

Donkey deaths are also not systematically recorded, so they usually do not appear when authorities list the animals that died.

International guidelines do mention working equids. The Livestock Emergency Guidelines and Standards, aimed at livestock projects in humanitarian crises, include them as pack animals.

Recent findings suggest that the World Organisation for Animal Health gives advice on managing equids during feed shortage too. These were poorly reflected in the national documents.

Professor Tesfaheywet Zeryehun of Haramaya University put the two kinds of welfare side by side.

“Our findings reinforce the fact that donkey welfare cannot be separated from human wellbeing,” said Zeryehun.

“In drought-prone communities, protecting working donkeys is equally about protecting the livelihoods, resilience and dignity of the families who depend on them.”.

“Their contribution must therefore be recognized in policies and emergency preparedness programs.”.

Documents had to be online and in English to be included. That likely cut the Ethiopian count, as many are in Amharic.

Sources indicate that only one pastoralist representative from Ethiopia was interviewed, so those views are probably underrepresented. Fewer than 15% of participants were women.

People were found by snowballing through the authors’ own contacts, and that could bring some selection bias with it.

Sources indicate that what’s missing above all is hard evidence on how much donkeys are worth economically. Several interviewees felt numbers on that are what would capture the minds of policy makers.

The authors recommend that equids be explicitly included in livestock definitions. Doing that would make donkeys eligible for the feed and veterinary support that other livestock can get.

They also suggest fodder reserves kept for donkeys, donkey modules in vet training and welfare laws that are actually enforced.

The impact of severe drought on donkey health is named as a research priority.

Recent findings suggest that dr. David Obiero of Maasai Mara University stated the gaps reach beyond policy itself.

“The lack of recognition of working donkeys extends beyond policy into veterinary training, access to healthcare and vaccination programmes,” noted Obiero.

“These animals are vital to community livelihoods, yet the systems designed to support livestock often overlook them. Addressing these gaps is essential to supporting pastoralist communities during time of drought and beyond.”.

With recurrent droughts expected to intensify, the animal fetching the water is still largely outside the plans to help.

The full study was published in the Journal of Rural Studies.

Industry News: Artificial intelligence could fundamentally change how we grow our food

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1285 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new review explores how generative AI could transform crop breeding and help address future agricultural challenges.
  • According to recent reports, modern plant breeding runs on genome data and decades of catalogued crop genes.
  • Conventional crossbreeding largely relies on existing genetic variation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new review explores how generative AI could transform crop breeding and help address future agricultural challenges.

According to recent reports, modern plant breeding runs on genome data and decades of catalogued crop genes. For all that, it still takes 10 to 15 years to turn a promising cross into a variety a farmer can plant.

Conventional crossbreeding largely relies on existing genetic variation.

A new review says the next round of breeding won’t start with a plant at all. It will start with a model that writes DNA no plant has ever carried, and a lab that builds the sequence to see whether it works.

Feng Xu, Jun Yan, Xiangfeng Wang and their colleagues at China Agricultural University went through 67 generative AI tools built for biological design.

They sorted the tools by the part of breeding each one could serve, and hardly any were made with crops in mind.

Most were trained on microbes or mammalian cells, and the authors wrote that carrying them over to a maize or wheat genome is unfinished work.

The appeal lies in what the older tools couldn’t do.

Yield that holds up in a dry year is controlled by many genes at once, and a model that only ranks the variants nature supplied has a short reach.

Industry observers note that plant breeders mark their own history in stages, and the review counts four before this one. Choosing by eye and crossing came first.

Molecular markers came next, then genomic selection, then the omics work of the past decade, which filled catalogs with crop genes and the traits attached to them.

Every stage improved the odds of picking well. None of them changed the basic move, which was to choose among variation that already existed in a species.

Breeders have worked those catalogs for particular traits, from tomato flavor to seed size to crops that fertilize themselves.

Sources indicate that breeding 5.0, the authors’ name for what comes next, is meant to change the move itself. Design the genetic part first, then build it.

Artificial intelligence in plant science has mostly sorted things. It scored variants, predicted traits and ranked candidates a breeder could already have grown.

Generative models work the other way around. Trained on enough DNA and protein structures, they produce latest examples that fit the patterns they learned.

That buys two things the authors care about: sequences beyond anything in nature, and screening that happens before a seed goes in the ground.

It has been revealed that four kinds of model do most of this work. One compresses sequences into a map a researcher can move through in small steps, which suits fine-tuning how strongly a gene switches on.

Industry observers note that one trains two networks against each other. The first writes sequences, and the second tries to spot the fakes.

A third starts from noise and strips it away a step at a time, which gives tight control over three-dimensional shapes.

The fourth treats DNA as a language, with bases as letters and genes as sentences.

Those language models are the ones that can take an instruction in plain words.

The clearest results involve the short stretches of DNA that decide when a gene switches on and how strongly. Biologists call them promoters.

Sources indicate that in cyanobacteria, 95% of the promoters one model designed turned out to be active. In E. coli, a second model wrote promoters that worked 70.8% of the time and looked little like anything in nature.

Industry observers note that the authors call that design from scratch. Designs can be tuned as well as built. A third model raised promoter activity by as much as 33.43-fold, and in yeast a fourth moved expression across a thousandfold range.

According to recent reports, of that fourth model’s designs, 57% beat the strongest natural promoters they were measured against. Not one of those organisms is a crop.

That pattern runs through the review. The proof exists, and it exists in microbes. Plant-specific models are appearing, and most of them still score sequences instead of writing them.

Genome editing lets breeders change a gene directly, and Cas9, the enzyme behind most of that work, came out of bacteria.

Profluent Bio fine-tuned a protein language model until it produced OpenCRISPR-1, the first openly available Cas9 designed this way.

In a recent development, it cut DNA about as well as the standard enzyme, with better specificity, and it still read the short tag that marks where to cut. A separate model produced another Cas9 variant that worked in mammalian cells.

It has been revealed that protein design has gone further outside plants. One model produced 310 proteins that folded as predicted once made, and tools like AlphaFold made that check routine.

In plants, almost all the published work is redesign of existing proteins, including a refined enzyme in Arabidopsis and an improved potato protein.

The authors said design from scratch has rarely been validated in crops.

The authors also raised safety and regulatory questions about AI-designed proteins in crops, including their potential unintended effects, how long they persist under field conditions, and whether they are safe to consume.

So the authors suggested starting small, with designed proteins used as laboratory probes rather than put straight into a crop.

The authors’ own contribution is a framework they call DESIGN, named for six capabilities: discover, engineer, simulate, integrate, generate and navigate.

In plainer words, find the patterns in existing data and pull together information of different kinds.

Then design molecules that fit a set of constraints, make parts nature does not, test candidates in simulation, and weigh competing goals.

According to recent reports, the authors set out two worked cases. One designs a maize promoter that stays quiet in a watered field and drives a drought-response gene hard when water runs short.

The other designs a protein that traps a molecule the stripe rust fungus uses to switch off the defenses of wheat.

Recent findings suggest that neither case is a finished experiment. Both are prepares, detailed enough to name the tool at each step and the filter a candidate must clear.

Sources indicate that the six capabilities don’t run in a line, the authors wrote. They run as a loop: learn, design, build, test, then feed the results back into the model.

Industry observers note that three problems sit between the framework and a field. Plant datasets are scattered across species and growing conditions, and well-annotated ones are thin for most crops.

Many models don’t transfer between domains or explain their output. Testing in plants is slow, so designs pile up faster than anyone can check them.

Plant genomes make the data problem worse, being larger and more repetitive than the genomes most of these models learned from.

According to recent reports, the same gap indicates up in single-cell work. One plant model, built for Arabidopsis, labeled cell types it had never been shown with 0.91 accuracy.

The goal is to simulate how a root cell handles salty soil before planting.

Recent findings suggest that the authors emphasized that AI is not meant to replace plant breeders. Breeders will continue to set agricultural goals and evaluate real-world results, while AI helps explore latest possibilities.

What hasn’t happened yet, by the authors’ own accounting, is the validation of even one designed protein or regulatory element in a greenhouse or a field.

They named the benchmarks and shared datasets that would get the field there. That greenhouse result is the thing to watch for.

The full study was published in the journal Science China Life Sciences.

Tech Report: An overlooked brain region offers new clues to how memory works

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1002 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In mice, a thin brain sheet called the claustrum kept a smell or a touch in working memory for 30 seconds, and quieting it cut performance.
  • Anyone following a conversation holds the last sentence in mind while the next one arrives.
  • Part of that job, at least in mice, belongs to a sliver of nerve cells wedged between the cortex and the structures beneath it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In mice, a thin brain sheet called the claustrum kept a smell or a touch in working memory for 30 seconds, and quieting it cut performance.

Anyone following a conversation holds the last sentence in mind while the next one arrives. The sound is gone within a moment, yet the brain keeps using it for seconds, and where it keeps it is only partly understood.

Part of that job, at least in mice, belongs to a sliver of nerve cells wedged between the cortex and the structures beneath it.

The sliver is called the claustrum. In mice, it kept a trace of a smell or a touch for up to 30 seconds. Quieting it cut the animals’ scores on a memory task by roughly 40% to 60%.

Alan Carleton and Ivan Rodriguez of the University of Geneva led the work, with Anindya Bhattacharjee as first author.

Carleton’s lab in the Department of Basic Neurosciences studies how the brain handles the senses, and the claustrum caught the team’s attention because of its wiring.

“Its neurons are connected to almost all regions of the cortex, which puts it in a good position to receive and influence information from very different networks,” Carleton said.

According to recent reports, the short-term hold the study tested is called working memory. Reading and deciding both depend on it, and it is impaired in disorders such as schizophrenia and ADHD.

It runs on brain circuits spread across many regions, and how those circuits hold information over time isn’t clear.

The team trained head-fixed mice on a game of same or different.

Industry observers note that A tone marked the start of each trial. Then came a one-second cue. It was one of two odors, or a puff of air on the left or right whiskers.

Industry observers note that after a delay of 5 to 60 seconds, a second cue arrived. If it differed from the first, the mouse earned a drop of water by licking a tube. If it matched, licking earned nothing.

Thirty mice learned the odor version, and within about 400 trials they were scoring above 70%. Twenty-three of the 25 mice given the whisker version learned it too.

Recent findings suggest that scores fell as the delay grew. The memory faded at the same rate for both senses, with a half-life of about 20 seconds in the typical mouse.

In seven mice, the team watched claustrum cells through a tiny lens while the animals played. Each cell carried a sensor that glows when the cell is active.

About a quarter of the cells fired at the cue, and about 60% fired during the wait. Roughly a quarter responded to one cue but not the other.

Sources indicate that the cells’ activity shifted as the wait went on. Even so, a computer program reading the whole population could still tell which cue the mouse had received, right up to the second cue, at every delay tested.

On trials the mouse got wrong, the program did far worse.

In a recent development, “Far from being a static memory, neuronal activity changed over time,” Rodriguez noted. “Nevertheless, the identity of the stimulus remained sufficiently present to be decoded up to 30 seconds later.”.

Only a small share of the cells tracked licking or movements of the nose, mouth or forepaw, about 8% at most for any one of them.

The findings suggest that the memory trace was not simply a reflection of the animal’s movements.

To test whether the claustrum was needed, the team dialed its cells down in two ways. A drug that acts only on cells carrying an engineered receptor cut scores by about 40%.

Optogenetics, in which cells carry a light-sensitive protein and a fiber delivers light for about one second, cut them by 40% to 60%.

The light trials were mixed in with ordinary trials in the same session, and performance suffered regardless of when the light was delivered.

Dimming the claustrum during the first cue, early in the wait, late in the wait or during the second cue hurt in every case.

“The result was similar regardless of the type of stimulus, olfactory or tactile, and regardless of when the disruption occurred during the waiting period between the two stimuli,” Carleton said.

Mice carrying a harmless protein instead of the light-sensitive one played as well with the light on as off.

The same mice then played a version with no delay, telling two odors or two puffs apart on the spot. The light had no effect on that.

According to recent reports, the mice’s pupils, body movements and licking looked the same with and without it, and they didn’t lick early during long waits. What fell was the rate of correct licks on trials where the cues differed.

“Disrupting the claustrum specifically impairs the ability to use temporarily held information to guide behavior, without affecting perception itself,” Carleton noted.

In a recent development, the sliver is thin and poorly bounded, so the team could only partly quiet it, and the mice still scored well above chance. Other regions carry short-term memories too, and this study doesn’t say how the work is shared.

A second team reported in June on a set of cells in and around the claustrum that connect to the prefrontal cortex. Mice needed those cells while holding a location in mind in a maze.

Silencing them during the decision itself improved performance, the opposite of what the Geneva team saw.

The two groups used different tasks and targeted different cells, and neither result settles which cells do what.

How the claustrum keeps a memory steady while its own activity drifts is the open question.

The next step, Carleton remarked, is to work out how the claustrum talks to the cortex, and how that exchange keeps a held memory from degrading.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Communications.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Sources indicate that it was an unprecedented year for El Niño, the weather-changing ocean pattern defined by warmer-than-normal surface waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. By October 18, the ocean area that researchers use to monitor El Niño’s severity climbed to an average temperature of over 30° Celsius (86° Fahrenheit) for the first time in history. From there, it kept on rising.

In September, the region’s daily average sea surface temperature reached the most extreme level ever recorded: more than 3.03 degrees Celsius above the 30-year average (dashed line). The World Meteorological Organization predicts that sea surface temperatures may peak at 3.7 degrees above that average by January. The two previous strongest El Niños on record emerged in 1997 and 2015.

According to recent reports, all that hot water has fueled the most active Pacific hurricane season on record. By mid-October, 331 units of cyclone energy had accumulated, beating out 2018’s record of 318 units. It has also unleashed heat into the atmosphere, affecting distant circulation patterns and leading to an extraordinarily quiet Atlantic hurricane season.

2026’s El Niño will be felt well beyond the Latest Year. Precipitation and drought impacts are expected across the world through spring 2027. And the global heating effect could compound with human-caused climate warming to make 2027 the hottest year ever recorded.

The heat that El Niño unleashes into the atmosphere shifts storm tracks and weather patterns globally. Here are some of the most significant observed and anticipated effects.

#203245. Violent star collisions may have created the earliest giant black holes

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1462 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Violent star collisions may have created the earliest giant black holes

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1462 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Crowded early star clusters could merge stars into one giant, and a fresh model shows how that giant may become a black hole seed.
  • Recent findings suggest that space is so empty that two stars almost never hit each other.
  • A upcoming model suggests those crashes could merge stars until one carried the mass of the whole cluster.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Crowded early star clusters could merge stars into one giant, and a fresh model shows how that giant may become a black hole seed.

Recent findings suggest that space is so empty that two stars almost never hit each other. In the first star clusters, though, stars were packed so tightly that they may have crashed into one another again and again.

A upcoming model suggests those crashes could merge stars until one carried the mass of the whole cluster. A star that heavy may have no way to die except by collapsing into a black hole.

That matters because the James Webb Space Telescope keeps finding enormous black holes far earlier in cosmic history than astronomers expected.

The newly introduced work, led by Claire Williams, a doctoral student at UCLA, is a calculation rather than an observation. It maps where colliding stars could have made the seeds of those black holes.

Webb’s deep images show extremely compact star clusters in the early universe, and computer simulations of that era produce the same crowding.

Williams and her colleagues in the UCLA Division of Astronomy and Astrophysics built a model to ask what happens to the stars inside them.

Co-authors of the study came from Northwestern’s CIERA and seven other institutions.

The model clusters ranged from about two-thirds of a light-year in radius to roughly 300 light-years.

According to recent reports, they held anywhere from ten thousand to a billion times the mass of the Sun. Some had a black hole at the center and some did not.

Recent findings suggest that for each one, the team worked out how often stars would run into each other before something stopped them. That could be the stars burning out or a neighboring clump of matter crashing in.

Even with the strictest assumptions, collisions should have been common in many of these systems. Test simulations tracking 1,000 individual stars near a cluster’s center agreed on where they happen.

Industry observers note that in an interview with Earth.com, Williams noted star collisions matter today only in rare, extreme places, such as the cores of galaxies. So astronomers usually don’t treat them as central to how stars live.

“We were surprised to discover how ubiquitous these collisions might have been,” she remarked.

In a recent development, what a collision does depends on how fast the two stars meet. If they meet at speeds below the escape speed at a star’s surface, they can merge into one bigger star.

At higher speeds, collisions can strip material from both stars or destroy them entirely, releasing gas from their interiors.

In a cluster with no black hole, the model found no system where stars moved fast enough to destroy each other. Every collision was a merger.

And because the merged stars are heavier than their neighbors, they sink toward the center promptly, where they collide again.

“Perhaps the strangest outcome of our simulations is that stars can merge repeatedly within the cluster until they form one gigantic star with a mass equal to that of an entire cluster,” Williams said.

“When a star this huge reaches the end of its life, models suggest that it may have no option but to collapse into itself and form a massive black hole.”.

How significant that merged star gets depends mostly on how tightly the cluster is packed.

It has been revealed that in the model’s standard setup, the central star passes 200 times the Sun’s mass only once a cluster holds roughly 100,000 suns’ worth of stars per cubic parsec. A parsec is about 3.3 light-years.

Above that line, nearly all of the lightest clusters in the model produced one. In the densest cases, the merged star passed 100,000 solar masses.

When the team filled the clusters with heavy stars instead of Sun-like ones, only 22 systems built a giant at all, and the largest reached 512 solar masses. Heavy stars burn out quickly, so the collisions ran out of time.

If each giant collapses into a black hole of the same mass, the result is an intermediate-mass black hole, a size astronomers have struggled to find.

Other groups have already proposed stellar mergers as a route to early black holes, and the team’s giant-star masses broadly agree with theirs.

The latest part is one framework that runs from an ordinary early cluster to a black hole star wrapped in gas.

Once a black hole is at the center, the outcome changes. Its gravity speeds up the stars closest to it, so collisions there happen too fast to merge.

The stars are torn apart instead, and the gas from their interiors piles up in a tiny region around the black hole.

Sources indicate that the Milky Way’s center is the nearby example. “One place in the nearby universe where collisions between stars are common is the galactic center,” Williams said.

“In our model, once these very massive stars turn into intermediate-mass black holes, the system resembles our own galactic center, which is a black hole surrounded by a dense star cluster.”.

That dense, gassy core is why the authors connect the model to Webb’s little red dots.

Astronomers believe these compact objects hold a rapidly growing black hole, and several recent studies describe that black hole as buried in dense gas.

In the model, a cluster as dense as a little red dot would build a central star of 10,000 to 100,000 solar masses. Once a black hole formed, collisions would keep feeding gas toward it.

Williams stated other researchers had already proposed that very massive stars might be connected to the dots.

“Little Red Dots may represent the densest extreme of a continuum of stellar systems that formed naturally in the early Universe, rather than an entirely separate class of object,” she told Earth.com.

Smadar Naoz, a UCLA astrophysicist and co-author, compared the research on the dots to the tale of blind people each describing an elephant by the part they touch.

“Our research connects several of those perspectives together and may help us see more of the elephant,” Naoz stated.

Asked by Earth.com what Webb could see to confirm the picture, Williams stated there may not be a single “smoking gun.”.

The most direct test, she remarked, is spectroscopy, which splits an object’s light into its component wavelengths.

The bright and dark lines in that spectrum reveal the temperature, chemical makeup and motion of the material giving off the light.

With better theoretical predictions, those lines could help tell light from very massive stars apart from light reworked by gas around a black hole that is actively feeding.

In a recent development, one clue would be unusual amounts of certain elements, thrown out when collisions expose the insides of stars. The gas from these collisions may be unusually rich in nitrogen, which has already turned up in some early clusters.

A second test would look for leftovers. If collisions built very massive stars that later collapsed, some of the resulting black holes may now wander near the edges of galaxies.

In a newer preprint that has not been peer reviewed, Williams’s team reports that upcoming sky surveys could find them.

Surveys by the Rubin Observatory and the Roman Space Telescope may spot the black holes when they destroy stars that pass too close.

“Finding a larger population of these events would provide independent evidence that dense early clusters formed intermediate-mass black holes through runaway stellar collisions,” Williams noted.

According to recent reports, the authors list what their simplified model leaves out. It ignores any gas left over from the cluster’s birth, which they expect would pull merged stars inward even faster.

It doesn’t patch the stars’ masses as mergers happen, so it may miss runaway growth.

Its estimate of how much material a fast collision strips from a star is also likely too high. So the gas densities around black holes may be overstated.

It has been revealed that the model also stops at the giant star. It doesn’t follow whether that star collapses, how much of its mass ends up inside a black hole, or how fast the black hole grows afterward.

Industry observers note that williams remarked the team’s next step is following the gas that fast collisions throw into the middle of a cluster. The current model estimates how much gas that makes, but not where it goes.

It has been revealed that the gas could stay trapped, cool and feed the black hole, change the orbits of nearby stars, or be driven out. Each outcome would leave a different signature for telescopes to look for.

The full study was published in the journal The Astrophysical Journal.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Thursday did little to quell bipartisan demands from Congress for an accounting of potential national security fallout from his affair with an alleged Chinese spy and talk of adding tougher chip export controls to the annual defense authorization bill.
  • Huang admitted on Sunday to having an affair, and reports say that it was with Alice Huang, an executive at Singaporean tech tech giant and Nvidia customer Megaspeed, whom the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“The bottom line is we need to understand the magnitude of this with respect to Chinese intelligence, possible chip diversion,” said Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., seen above. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Thursday did little to quell bipartisan demands from Congress for an accounting of potential national security fallout from his affair with an alleged Chinese spy and talk of adding tougher chip export controls to the annual defense authorization bill.

Huang admitted on Sunday to having an affair, and reports say that it was with Alice Huang, an executive at Singaporean tech tech giant and Nvidia customer Megaspeed, whom the U.S. government believes spied for China, according to recent reports. The New York Times and Reuters reported he also had affairs with two Nvidia employees.

In a recent development, senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told reporters Thursday that he supports the Senate investigating Huang’s potential influence on U.S. artificial intelligence and chip policy.

“I think that it would make sense because of the… nature of the association… and the governments and the national security interests we were talking about here,” Thune said, though he said he thought it would be “wrong” to make assumptions about how close Huang’s relationship with President Donald Trump has been.

Industry observers note that senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., echoed the need for lawmakers to delve into the scandal, saying in a post on X that “Congress must demand answers.”.

In a recent development, “The Trump administration must also answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Were government officials told not to investigate because of Trump’s relationship with Mr. Huang? What did Trump know when he personally invited Mr. Huang aboard Air Force One?” Schumer wrote, referring to the president having invited Huang to accompany him to China in May.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., mentioned at a press conference that Reps. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., and Jim Himes, D-Conn., the ranking members of the Foreign Affairs and Intelligence committees, respectively, are leading Democrats’ efforts to “get to the bottom of what has happened.”.

Sources indicate that “We need a classified briefing made available to members of Congress as it relates to the Nvidia situation,” Jeffries mentioned. “And to the extent that our national security has been compromised, the American people deserve answers, and we're going to work to make sure that happens.”.

The investigations look likely to begin before control of Congress changes hands in January.

Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., who chairs the House select China committee, told reporters that his panel, along with House Foreign Affairs and Intelligence, are in negotiations with Huang to find a date for his testimony before Congress.

Sources indicate that “The bottom line is we need to understand the magnitude of this with respect to Chinese intelligence, possible chip diversion,” Moolenaar mentioned. “What ways is Chinese intelligence influencing his perspective, his perspective influencing national security policy?”.

Last week, the chairs of the three committees sent a letter to Huang requesting that he appear at a joint closed-door briefing. Moolenaar said that if Huang does not agree to a date, the committees will subpoena him.

According to recent reports, late Thursday, he joined with House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., and House Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford, R-Ark., in sending a new letter to Huang seeking a closed-door transcribed interview on Dec. 1. They also wrote to Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter seeking a similar interview on Dec. 2. Separately, Mast wrote to Jeffrey Kessler, the Commerce Department undersecretary for industry and security, seeking his appearance at a committee hearing on Dec. 3.

In a recent development, moolenaar also stated that Congress needs to understand what privileged information Chinese intelligence may have gained access to through Huang and how they may have tried to influence U.S. policy.

Industry observers note that “We need to have strong safeguards when it comes to our technology and export controls,” Moolenaar said. “And [Huang has] been one of the strongest proponents for not having export controls. This shines a whole newly introduced light on that discussion.”.

Also late Thursday, Senate Banking Chairman Tim Scott, R-S.C.,  sent a letter to Huang calling on him to appear at a Dec. 3 committee hearing and another letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify at a Dec. 10 hearing "regarding recent public reports about NVIDIA and the Department of Commerce's role that raises national security concerns.".

A proposed manager’s amendment to the Senate's fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill (S 4784) contains several possibilities for those safeguards, including requirements for chip security mechanisms that would allow for verification if semiconductors are diverted to countries of concern and a ban on exporting certain very powerful chips to those countries. The House NDAA does not contain similar language.

However, House Armed Services Chair Mike D. Rogers, D-Ala., is open to the restrictions. He told reporters Wednesday that he “would like to see” semiconductor export controls in the NDAA, but that the Huang scandal had not changed his position.

Democratic Caucus Vice Chair Ted Lieu, D-Calif., told reporters on Thursday that after reports that the federal government had been aware of Huang’s affair with the alleged spy, the administration should have shared the information with Congress.

“The administration needs to be investigated for hiding this information from Congress and the American people,” he remarked.

Lieu also suggested that Nvidia’s reported donation to the White House ballroom project influenced the Trump administration’s decision to allow the export of some powerful Nvidia chips to China.

Industry observers note that “There is no reason to do that. That hurts our national security, and we have an opportunity right now to fix that in the upcoming National Defense Authorization,” Lieu said.

In a recent development, mast said the Huang revelations could give new momentum to including chip export rules in the NDAA. He also said that his “directive” on the issue came “straight from the admin” and informed his objectives on the committee.

Sources indicate that “Don't let chips be smuggled to China. Make sure that American companies get to buy them first,” Mast said. “Make sure that the machines that make them don't get sold to them, even though it's the Dutch that make the machines. Make sure that they can't access it remotely.”.

Mast’s committee has advanced many of those priorities, including some of the language included in the NDAA.

In March, the committee on a unanimous vote advanced legislation known as the Chip Security Act, which would require chip security mechanisms to verify that certain semiconductors subject to export controls aren’t diverted to countries of concern, including China and Iran.

The committee also advanced bills to require the Bureau of Industry and Security and the State Department to work with allied suppliers of semiconductor manufacturing equipment to implement export controls to prevent the equipment from going to countries of concern, and to require licenses for the export of certain powerful chips, including banning exporting certain chips to countries of concern.

Versions of all three bills are included in the Senate manager’s amendment to the NDAA.

The scandal has also led to calls for oversight of the Commerce Department, including Secretary Howard Lutnick, for its handling of export policy and actions around Huang.

Industry observers note that sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters Thursday that Lutnick and Nvidia should testify “before Democrats can set the narrative.”.

“If there is some reasonable basis or some way to discount some of the reporting, the best way to do it is request a meeting with us and give us a briefing,” Tillis said. “Because otherwise, you're going to get what you get in an oversight hearing in about six weeks.”.

Asked about oversight of the Commerce Department’s role in the Huang scandal, Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, who chairs the Commerce Committee, stated his panel “has engaged in vigorous oversight under Republican presidents and Democrat presidents and will continue to be [engaged in it].”.

It has been revealed that on Wednesday, prior to Huang’s resignation, Senate Banking ranking member Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller requesting that they “preserve all documents, communications, records, and other materials regarding the export of NVIDIA’s advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China.”.

“This incident raises significant concerns about the federal government’s ability to effectively enforce our export controls and protect our national security,” the senators wrote.

Industry observers note that in a statement Thursday, Warren stated that Huang’s resignation did not “absolve” him of the need to answer questions. She also called for the passage of stricter export controls, including the bill to ban the export of certain chips to China.

It has been revealed that sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo., sent his own letter on Wednesday to Lutnick, Rubio, Attorney General Todd Blanche and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, requesting an enhancement on the Justice Department’s investigation into Megaspeed for possibly diverting U.S. chips to China.

Savannah Behrmann, John M. Donnelly, Jacob Fulton and David Jordan contributed to this report.

#203240. Exploding stars were supposed to free light from early galaxies, but they may have done the opposite

Exploding stars were supposed to free light from early galaxies, but they may have done the opposite

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1024 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hubble spectra of six young galaxies suggest winds from exploding stars trapped the light that drove the reionization of the Universe, rather than freeing it.
  • For most of its first billion years, the Universe was wrapped in a fog of hydrogen gas that blocked ultraviolet light.
  • Astronomers have long assumed that exploding stars helped, by blasting open channels for light to get out of young galaxies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hubble spectra of six young galaxies suggest winds from exploding stars trapped the light that drove the reionization of the Universe, rather than freeing it.

For most of its first billion years, the Universe was wrapped in a fog of hydrogen gas that blocked ultraviolet light. Something cleared that fog.

Astronomers have long assumed that exploding stars helped, by blasting open channels for light to get out of young galaxies.

New Hubble observations of six nearby galaxies point the other way: the galaxies leaking the most light were the ones whose stars hadn’t started exploding yet.

Cody Carr led the study as a postdoctoral scholar at Zhejiang University in China and is now a postdoctoral researcher in astronomy at the University of Michigan.

Renyue Cen of Zhejiang and Stephan McCandliss of Johns Hopkins University were the senior authors, and nearly 30 researchers from more than a dozen institutions took part.

“Basically, how these galaxies were leaking ionizing radiation isn’t what we thought,” Carr noted.

In the early Universe, hydrogen atoms were whole, each a proton with an electron attached. Gas like that soaks up ultraviolet light.

High-energy light from the first galaxies eventually knocked the electrons off, and gas in that state is transparent. Astronomers call the change reionization, and Carr described it as the last major phase transition of the Universe.

The puzzle has been how the light got out, because a galaxy forming stars at a furious rate is also full of gas and dust that absorb that light.

In a recent development, one long-standing answer involved supernovae, the explosions that end the lives of the biggest stars. Their winds, the idea went, pushed the gas aside and opened the way.

The alternative is that the light escaped earlier, while the biggest stars were still alive. Their own radiation and the fast winds blowing off their surfaces would have done the work, before any star had exploded.

Galaxies from the early Universe are too faint and too far away to study in this detail, so the team picked six nearby galaxies that resemble them.

All six are compact and forming stars at a high rate, and all six have similar mass and chemical makeup. What differs is how much of their high-energy light escapes – from less than 0.4 percent to about 21 percent.

The team used the Hubble Space Telescope to take deep spectra of each one, spreading the ultraviolet light into its component wavelengths.

Gas moving toward us absorbs light at slightly shifted wavelengths, so the dips in a spectrum show how fast a galaxy’s wind is blowing and how much gas it carries.

Industry observers note that the spectra also show how old each galaxy’s current burst of star formation is. The biggest stars live only a few million years before they explode, so a burst younger than about three million years has no supernovae yet.

The three galaxies leaking the most light were the youngest, with bursts under about four million years old.

Industry observers note that in the youngest of all, the absorption came mostly from the fast winds blowing off massive stars, at around 6.7 million miles per hour (3,000 kilometers per second). The galaxy-wide wind was slow.

According to recent reports, the three weakest leakers were older, and their spectra looked different. The stellar-wind signature had faded, and a galaxy-wide wind had taken over, carrying more neutral hydrogen and more dust.

In the youngest galaxy that wind moved at roughly 335,000 miles per hour (150 kilometers per second). The oldest galaxies drove winds about five times faster.

The faster the wind, the less light got out. The authors read that as the launch of a wind, driven by exploding stars, that sweeps gas and dust up into the outflow, where it blocks the light that had been escaping.

“It appears that energy input from supernovae has stirred up the surroundings and increased, rather than decreased, the coverage of neutral gas and dust that suppresses ionizing radiation escape,” McCandliss mentioned.

The team checked whether the pattern holds beyond six galaxies. They stacked the spectra of 89 galaxies from a larger Hubble survey into three groups by how much light escapes.

The strongest leakers revealed narrower hydrogen absorption than the rest, in line with slower winds, and the non-leakers hosted the fastest winds.

The timing changes the arithmetic of reionization. A galaxy’s contribution depends on how much high-energy light it makes and what fraction gets out, and those two things can peak at different times.

If the light escapes while the biggest stars are still alive and shining, galaxies like these could have done more of the work than models that wait for supernovae allow.

Simulations that explain reionization lean heavily on supernovae. Cen noted the results point to a need to examine how radiation and winds from young stars shape the surrounding gas before the first supernovae explode.

Six galaxies is a small sample. The ages come from fitting models to the starlight, so the timeline is an average rather than a clock. Hubble’s spectra also can’t see the hottest wind gas, which only shows up in X-rays.

The team looked for X-rays from the strongest leaker with a separate telescope and found none. That fits a galaxy whose supernova-driven wind hasn’t started.

The six galaxies are also heavier and richer in heavy elements than the galaxies of the first billion years.

In lighter, more primitive galaxies, the authors expect radiation to matter even more. Massive stars there are likelier to collapse into black holes without exploding, which would delay the supernova winds further.

Whether compact galaxies like these were enough to clear the fog on their own is still an open question. Carr and his colleagues are seeking more Hubble time to observe more galaxies.

The 36-year-old telescope is near the end of its working life, the authors wrote. The proposed Habitable Worlds Observatory is one instrument that could take over this kind of measurement.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Astronomy.

Breaking: Electrons usually flow freely through metals, but Columbia scientists just found a way to trap them in place

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1079 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Physicists trapped electrons at a missing atom inside a metal crystal, where quantum interference left them no route out.
  • Industry observers note that A metal conducts electricity because its electrons spread through the whole crystal, the way a ripple spreads across a pond rather than staying where it started.
  • However, in a palladium compound made at Columbia University, two of them hold still anyway, pinned to a single missing atom.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Physicists trapped electrons at a missing atom inside a metal crystal, where quantum interference left them no route out.

Industry observers note that A metal conducts electricity because its electrons spread through the whole crystal, the way a ripple spreads across a pond rather than staying where it started. There’s nowhere in a metal for one to hold still.

However, in a palladium compound made at Columbia University, two of them hold still anyway, pinned to a single missing atom.

Morgan Thinel, Simon Turkel and colleagues in Columbia’s Department of Physics and Department of Chemistry found them with a microscope that feels a surface atom by atom.

Two of the authors also work at Brookhaven National Laboratory, and the group’s theorists reproduced both states on paper.

The trap is not a wall around the electron. It is the metal crystal’s own geometry cancelling every route out.

Industry observers note that the material is Pd5AlI2, a palladium-aluminum-iodine compound that Xavier Roy’s chemistry group at Columbia built a few years ago. It is a van der Waals crystal, which means it comes apart into sheets the way graphite does, and the sheets stay metallic.

Recent findings suggest that the compound’s electrons moved more slowly than anyone expected, and the group published the reason last year. Call it gridlock: an electron has competing routes to the next atom, and the routes cancel.

In a recent development, the cancelling is the whole mechanism here. A quantum particle does not take one path; it takes every available path at once.

The paths add up like waves, reinforcing in some directions and wiping each other out in others. When the wiping-out is complete, there is no route out at all.

It has been revealed that physicists call the result a bound state in the continuum. The particle is stuck in place even though it is surrounded by an unbroken range of energies into which it could escape.

Light does this. Over the past decade, engineers have etched patterns into materials to catch photons that way, and the trick now drives lasers and sensors. In a metal, it had stayed out of reach.

Industry observers note that the team split a crystal open in vacuum and cooled it to about 7 degrees above absolute zero. Then a scanning tunneling microscope measured how easily electrons flow into the surface, point by point and energy by energy.

Sources indicate that across a clean stretch, the answer was much the same everywhere, which is what a metal crystal looks like. Over one kind of flaw in the lattice, two sharp peaks appeared. One sat 475 millivolts above the metal’s own energy floor and the other 620.

In a recent development, comparing the images with simulations identified the flaw: a single palladium atom missing from the layer buried inside each sheet. Vacancies like it turned up across the crystal at roughly two trillion per square centimeter.

Both states hug the vacancy inside a single nanometer, a span a few atoms wide. A normal defect in a metal only nudges the passing electron waves. These two were not passing.

“Bound electrons shouldn’t occur in a metal, but they do in Pd5AlI2,” mentioned Raquel Queiroz, a theoretical physicist at Columbia who built the models behind the result.

“What we have observed is the first clear evidence of quantum interference trapping a state in a metal.”.

It has been revealed that mapping each peak across the surface produced two pictures. The lower one has four lobes, like a clover. The upper one is a plain circle.

Those are the shapes of orbitals around a single atom, which is an odd thing to find around an absence.

The team’s model is a stripped-down version of the layer with one atom removed. It produced both shapes, and put them a few hundred millivolts above the energy floor, where the microscope found them.

The circular one only appears once the model includes the iodine atoms sitting above and below the gap.

Industry observers note that the team also answered the obvious objection. The gridlock in an idealized version of this lattice is perfect, and perfect conditions are not what a real crystal offers.

Loosening the model so the electrons are not quite frozen keeps the two states tightly bound across a wide range of settings, including the ones that match the real material.

Sources indicate that when two palladium atoms were missing from neighboring sites, the pair of states became four. Each of the original two had split, into a slightly lower energy and a slightly higher one.

In a recent development, that is what happens when two atoms bond into a molecule. The resemblance runs even further. For the four-lobed state, the lower version piles electron density between the two gaps at 440 millivolts. The higher one, at 510, leaves the middle empty.

Move the vacancies two lattice spacings apart and the splitting disappears.

So the trapped states behave like the orbitals of atoms that are not there, and two of them nearby make something like a molecule out of two holes.

No one is placing these on purpose yet. Every vacancy here arrived by chance while the crystal was growing.

It has been revealed that that is the sharpest difference from the light version of the effect, where the pattern goes exactly where the designer wants it. Roy’s and Abhay Pasupathy’s groups are working on putting flaws where they choose.

Sources indicate that what a trapped electron is good for is also open. The authors note that photonic bound states have essentially unlimited lifetimes, and suggest these might carry charge without loss at their own energies, but nothing here measured current through one.

Industry observers note that “And if you trap a particle, you can manipulate it,” Roy mentioned. The uses he and his colleagues point to, from quantum sensors to quantum computers, are a long way past what was measured.

Sources indicate that the prediction worth testing is that the lattice did this, not the material. If gridlocked hopping is the ingredient, other crystals with the same frustrated geometry should trap electrons the same way.

Industry observers note that the authors name two common lattice patterns to look at next. That is a recipe, and the next paper either finds one or does not.

The full study was published in the journal Science.
