📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that QR codes are everywhere when we travel now, on restaurant tables, parking meters, hotel signs, airports, train stations, and transit machines. This travel scam known as Quishing or QR code phishing is becoming the fastest growing travel scam warning out there. Most QR codes are legitimate, but scammers are using fake QR code stickers and fake payment pages to catch travellers when they are tired, rushed, or distracted.

According to recent reports, QR code travel scam happens when a fake QR code sends travellers to a fraudulent website. The code may be placed over a real QR code on a parking meter, restaurant table, hotel notice, airport sign, or transit machine, or it may arrive by text or email pretending to be a fine, toll, ticket, or check-in request. The safest rule is simple: Pause. Check. Then pay.Read out post: 20 Common Travel Scams and How to Avoid Them.

Industry observers note that A scammer does not always need to hack a system or damage a payment machine. Sometimes they print a fake QR code sticker and place it directly over a legitimate code.

From a quick glance, the sign still looks official. The logo may look familiar. The instructions may seem normal. The page that opens may copy the colours, layout, and branding of the real firm.

It has been revealed that you think you are paying for parking, ordering food, checking into a hotel, or settling a toll. Instead, criminals may be collecting your credit card number, password, phone number, licence plate, email address, or other personal information.

The FTC has also warned about fake traffic violation texts that begin with a QR code and try to scare people into paying a fake unpaid balance.

The FTC has warned that scammers hide harmful links in QR codes to steal personal information, including by placing fake QR codes over real ones on parking meters.

Many restaurants now use QR codes for menus, ordering, or payment. Most are legitimate, but travellers should still be cautious. This is the easiest travel scam for QR code phishing as everyone uses it.

It has been revealed that A menu QR code should usually show a menu. Be careful if it asks for information it does not need, such as your passport number, banking details, hotel room number, or a password.

Before scanning a QR code on a restaurant table, look at the surface. Does it look printed into the menu or table sign, or does it look like a sticker placed on top? If it looks raised, crooked, bubbled, or mismatched, ask staff for a printed menu or the restaurant’s official website.

Parking is one of the easiest places for this scam to work because travellers are often rushed and confused.

According to recent reports, you may not know the local parking app. You may be dealing with another language. You may be worried about getting a ticket. That pressure makes a “scan to pay” sticker feel helpful.

Before paying through a parking QR code, inspect the sticker, read the URL preview, and check whether the payment page matches the city, parking authority, or official app named on the machine.

If anything feels off, do not use the QR code. Type the official website yourself, use the official parking app, pay at the machine, or ask local staff for help.

Industry observers note that airports and transit stations are full of QR codes: Wi-Fi, directions, tickets, luggage storage, forms, lounge access, and service information. Travel scams often happen when travelers are in a hurry. If you need wifi, a taxi, some food, QR codes are often the easiest way to catch you off guard.

That does not mean every code is unsafe. It means you should slow down when a public QR code asks for payment, passwords, ID documents, or personal information.

According to recent reports, the FBI warns that malicious QR codes can send people to fake sites, steal victim data, embed malware, or redirect payments. The FBI warns that criminals can tamper with QR codes to redirect payments, steal login and financial information, or send people to malicious websites.

The easiest way to avoid this scam is to build one habit before you scan a public QR code.

Industry observers note that do not scan just because a sign looks official. Public signs, parking meters, table cards, and posters can be tampered with.

If the message claims you must pay immediately, avoid a fine, settle a toll, confirm a booking, or prevent a penalty, slow down. Urgency is one of the biggest warning signs.

Before your phone opens anything, look at the QR code itself.

In a recent development, we call this the scratch test. You are not damaging the sign. You are simply checking whether the QR code feels or looks different from the rest of the surface.

Canadian readers can also check the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security’s QR code safety guidance and report fraud through the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre.

Industry observers note that most phones show a preview of the website before opening the page. Read it.

Look for misspellings, extra words, strange endings, random letters, shortened links, or a domain that does not match the firm, hotel, restaurant, city, or attraction.

Do not rely only on the padlock symbol. A secure connection does not automatically mean the site is legitimate. The real question is whether you are on the correct website.

The FTC has also warned about fake traffic violation texts that include a QR code and pressure people to pay a fake unpaid balance.

For payments, passwords, account logins, or identity information, the safest option is often to bypass the QR code.

Sources indicate that open your browser and type the official website yourself. Use an app you already installed from the official app store. Ask an employee for the correct payment method. Contact your hotel, airline, rental car organization, or bank through the phone number on your booking or card — not through the number on a suspicious page.

Sources indicate that first, do not panic. Scanning a QR code does not automatically mean your information has been stolen. The bigger risk usually begins when you enter payment information, type a password, download a file, or provide personal details.

If you scanned a suspicious code:.

Close the page immediately if the link looks wrong, the message creates urgency, or the site asks for information you did not expect to provide.

Do not download an unfamiliar app or file from a QR code.

If you entered credit card information, contact your bank or card issuer using the official number on the back of your card or through the official banking app.

According to recent reports, if you entered a password, change it through the official website or app. If you reused that password anywhere else, change it there too.

Watch for follow-up messages. A scammer who has some of your information may later pretend to be your bank, hotel, airline, rental car tech giant, or payment provider.

Report the fake QR code to the business, parking authority, hotel, airport, or local authority so they can remove it.

A QR code may be suspicious if it looks like a sticker placed over another code, has peeling edges, opens a strange URL, uses a shortened link, creates urgency, asks for information that does not make sense, or directs you away from the official website or app.

Sources indicate that at a restaurant, a QR menu should not need your passport or banking password. At a parking meter, the payment page should match the city or parking authority. At a hotel, a check-in code should not send you to a random payment page outside the official booking system.

The BBB has also warned consumers to double-check QR codes before paying for parking.

No. QR codes are part of modern travel, and many are perfectly safe.

Recent findings suggest that the goal is not to panic every time you see one. The goal is to stop treating every QR code as automatically trustworthy.

A few seconds of inspection can protect you from a much longer financial or account-recovery problem later.

QR codes are convenient, but convenience is exactly what scammers are using against travellers.

Before scanning a public QR code at a restaurant, parking meter, hotel, airport, train station, attraction, or transit stop, remember the rule:.

Inspect the code. Read the link. Go directly to the official website or app when money, passwords, or personal information are involved.

That tiny pause may be the thing that saves your trip.

Scanning a QR code is not automatically dangerous. The danger usually begins when you open a suspicious page, enter payment details, type a password, download a file, or provide personal information without checking whether the site is legitimate.

According to recent reports, inspect the physical code for stickers, raised edges, bubbles, peeling corners, or anything placed over another code. Then check the URL preview before opening the page. If the link looks strange or does not match the official firm, city, hotel, or attraction, do not use it.

Before entering payment information, make sure the website belongs to the official business or authority. When in doubt, use the official app, type the website manually, pay directly at the machine, or ask staff for the correct payment method.

Contact your bank or card issuer immediately using the official number on the back of your card or your banking app. Watch for suspicious charges, replace the card if needed, and do not use any contact information from the suspicious website.

How I Got My Visa to France

📅 16 Feb 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1984 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nomadicmatt

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that I’ve been in love with France ever since my first trip to Bordeaux in 2010.
  • According to recent reports, but that love became an obsession when, after Bordeaux, I stepped out of the Paris metro and onto the Champs-Élysées.
  • In a recent development, since then, Paris has had a firm grip on my heart.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I’ve been in love with France ever since my first trip to Bordeaux in 2010. Friends I had met back in Thailand revealed me around the area and introduced me to French culture. It was my first time in France and I loved the food, the wine, and the people.

According to recent reports, but that love became an obsession when, after Bordeaux, I stepped out of the Paris metro and onto the Champs-Élysées. The lights, the energy, the mystique! There was magic in the air. I felt like I had known the city my entire life and I was simply returning home.

In a recent development, since then, Paris has had a firm grip on my heart. Over the years, I spent countless visits exploring France and Paris in particular. I’ve run tours in the city and I spent a few months living there in 2019.

Last August, after yet another sojourn, I thought to myself, “What if I moved back?”.

In a recent development, I was growing a bit tired of the NYC dating scene, the rising cost of living, and felt like, creatively, I was in a rut. With AI coming for creators like me and the industry changing, I was a little lost on what, career-wise, would come next.

And Paris seemed like the best place to go.

Sources indicate that it’s cheaper than NYC, I had friends there already, I’ve always wanted to learn French, it would make a great base for exploring Europe, and I could start writing my next book there. There’s nothing like a change in scenery to get the creativity flowing!

But the question remained: how do you move to France?

After all, they don’t have a digital nomad visa, and you’re limited to three months if you visit on your regular Schengen tourist visa.

In a recent development, well, it turns out that it’s not actually that hard. (And while I can only speak for Americans, I suspect the criteria are similar for Canadians, Aussies, Kiwis, and other “developed” nations.).

If you want to move to France, you have four main options:.

It has been revealed that the student visa is pretty straightforward. You need to enroll in a full-time university program and show you have enough funds to support yourself (around 600 Euros per month). A friend is currently there on this visa, as she is doing a nine-month intensive French program to become fluent. You still have to apply for the visa, but if you’re enrolled in an accredited school, you’ll likely get approved. Another benefit to this visa is that you can work part-time on it!

But this visa is contingent on being in school, so if you leave or quit, it’s voided. However, when you are done, you can change this to a “job seeker” visa, which can give you up to another six months in France (or more depending on how long your program was).

I thought about applying for the entrepreneur visa, but the application process is pretty complex and can take months to be approved. You have to set up your business in France — and that is a lot of paperwork. You have to show that your business makes money, has clients (at least one of them being French), and can support you full-time (you have to make at least the French minimum wage). They will scrutinize your assets and financials a lot and you’ll need to register your business in France and pay French taxes.

Additionally, France offers a talent visa. If you’re an expert in your field (with verifiable accreditations and accolades), this could be a good visa to apply for, especially if you blueprint to stay in France for a long time and want to physically work there. But, again, you’ll need to have some source of income and plan to do physical business in France. If you’re not an academic but someone in the arts, you have to show how you are going to add to the “culture of France” in some way.

While I would meet the requirements for both those visas, the process for either would have been time-consuming, and, since I’m not sure France is going to be my forever home, I decided not to go through that process.

So I went with the long-term visitor visa, officially called VLS-TS visiteur. This allows me to stay up to 12 months in France and is renewable in the country. It does come with a lot of restrictions, however: I can’t physically work here and I am not allowed into the French social welfare system.

Industry observers note that it’s also the visa a lot of Americans (and most retirees) are coming in on. If you have passive income or retirement savings and just want to live in France, this is a good option for you. It allows you to set up a bank account and it can be renewed pretty much indefinitely.

Industry observers note that the paperwork for this visa (which I’ll get into in a bit) essentially comes down to whether or not you can support yourself. French authorities want to make sure you won’t be a burden on the system.

My biggest question centered around whether or not I could “work” on this visa. A lot of creators and digital nomads are applying for — and getting — this visa.

But remember: you aren’t allowed to work on this visa so how are you going to work if you can’t work?

So let me take a moment to talk about “work” from a legal standpoint.

As I mentioned, there’s no digital nomad visa that allows you to work in France. And the French tax office said last July that remote work is considered taxable — but there are no official laws that say so. That’s just their opinion and there’s been no progress in codifying that opinion. In fact, my visa doesn’t even come with a tax number, so I can’t be taxed. I couldn’t pay taxes even if I wanted to.

The visa office asks how you’ll support yourself when you are in France and one of the sources of income they accept is “income from work.” I was very open that my means of support would be the income from this blog and my books.

The system there really hasn’t caught up to remote work. It still defines “work” as something you do physically that could take away a job from a French person.

In a recent development, so could I run walking tours in Paris? Nope. Could you work at a café? Nope.

In a recent development, but does writing this blog post count as work? After all, no one is paying for it. It’s a free resource. Does going to a café to work on the next great American novel count? What about my weekly newsletter that has affiliate links (that generate income) in it? Is writing that considered work?

Recent findings suggest that the gray area is considerable, so the best thing to do is to talk to a lawyer. I recommend Daniel Tostado (yes, that’s his real name), one of the biggest American-French immigration lawyers in Paris. He has a huge law firm and regularly meets with government officials to clarify the rules on this. He gave me some solid advice.

For this long-term visitor visa, the application process is pretty easy. You go to the French government website, fill out your application, take the application number to the TLScontact website, and make an appointment. (France outsources the appointment process to this organization, which then sends everything to the French consulate for approval.).

The main things you’ll want to demonstrate are that you have accommodation for 90 days on your application and enough income to support yourself. They just want to make sure you aren’t going to be a burden on the system. I went overboard. Here’s what I brought to my appointment:.

Industry observers note that I didn’t need the second bank account, tax returns, or W-2 (they weren’t required) but the woman at the appointment remarked the more proof you had the better and it wouldn’t hurt. And another friend who got this visa didn’t bring anything beyond what was asked in the application form. But I wanted to take no chances!

At the appointment, the staff double-checks your paperwork, takes your biometric data, collects the fees, and then sends your passport to the embassy for processing. Officially, it takes up to 15 days to process your visa, but everyone I know seems to get it back within a week.

According to recent reports, the worst part was not knowing if you are approved until your passport is returned. While you can track the progress of your application, you don’t know the verdict until your passport is back in your hands. While I was waiting (and anxiously spiraling), I looked on Reddit and found that most denials were for lack of income or problems with their accommodation, which seem to be the two most notable things to have perfect on your application.

Once you get your visa back, you can enter France any time after the start date. After you enter, you have 90 days to register your visa with the state (they give you a little QR code with instructions). This allows you to “officially” be on this long-term visa. (It’s a more paperwork kind of thing.).

Once that is done, there’s nothing else to do and you can stay in France (and Europe) until your visa expires!

Recent findings suggest that so, if you’re considering moving to France, these are your options. But, as always, I’m not a lawyer and this is not legal advice. In regard to work and other concerns or questions, it’s vital that you seek legal counsel and get their expert opinion!

#203097. The Golden Rules of Affordable Family Travel, Illustrated by Mona Chalabi

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2254 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

The Golden Rules of Affordable Family Travel, Illustrated by Mona Chalabi

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2254 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • My first Thanksgiving was a lavish 12-person dinner in Connecticut in 2014.
  • In a recent development, take it from an immigrant: this holiday is full of weird contradictions.
  • As we approach the last Thursday of November, with money very much on our minds, the below well-traveled parents share their hard-won wisdom on pulling off affordable family travel—including how to find treasure in New York City’s Chinatown without paying an arm and a leg, seek out free entertainment in the streets of Oaxaca, and embrace the joys of accessible public transportation in Europe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

My first Thanksgiving was a lavish 12-person dinner in Connecticut in 2014. I had moved to the US in March of that year and had planned on working from home until a friend generously invited me to go spend the day with her family; an act of unguarded openness that I’ve realized is one of the many things that differentiates Americans from Brits. As soon as we got off the train in Cambridge, Massachusetts, I realized that even though my friend lived in a nasty, overcrowded apartment in Brooklyn, she came from a family that had immense wealth. After dinner, as I helped wash plates in the kitchen, my friend’s mum asked her why she wouldn’t just move into the lovely building they had bought for her. She turned beet red and handed me another dirty plate without looking at me.

In a recent development, take it from an immigrant: this holiday is full of weird contradictions. Of course, there’s the annual reminder of colonization which requires a careful forgetting of the people who have been colonized. And then there’s the financial aspect of it. At first blush, it seems like the least capitalist holiday of the year—there isn’t the expense of Christmas or Hanukkah gift-giving or the extravagance of Halloween candy. Yet the holiday also marks the start of one of the year's busiest travel seasons when families are taking great expense to reunite, vacation, and explore outside of their every day lives.

As we approach the last Thursday of November, with money very much on our minds, the below well-traveled parents share their hard-won wisdom on pulling off affordable family travel—including how to find treasure in New York City’s Chinatown without paying an arm and a leg, seek out free entertainment in the streets of Oaxaca, and embrace the joys of accessible public transportation in Europe. All of these stories say something about the wealth of the person writing it, whether or not they wanted to reveal that information. I’m obsessed with getting to the truth about someone’s class (it’s why I wrote my book on the subject), and so these family dispatches, which serve as equal parts advice and confession, are a treat I’ll come back to when I’m not busy washing a rich family’s plates. —Mona Chalabi, Pulitzer Prize-winning writer and illustrator.

Keep reading for the tips and tricks of affordable family travel, road-tested by the experts and illustrated by Mona Chalabi.

I know the secret to parenting and I’m willing to share it: snacks. Snacks are everything—they’re an activity, a mood changer, and a window into culture for kids. Hit a local farmers market on your first day or if you’re somewhere truly out of their comfort zone even a local convenience store—like 7-Eleven in Tokyo—for something that can feel both familiar and novel. If your hotel room has a refrigerator you can store any pre-cut fruit that you buy, or opt for items that don’t require refrigeration like apples, bananas, and clementines. Bring a lightweight backpack, refill each morning, and watch the hangry meltdowns (mostly) vanish. —Dana Kravis, global executive director, CNT video.

Last December in London, we stayed in a quaint Airbnb in Primrose Hill and explored different neighborhoods on foot. When our kids, then eight and three, got tired, we hopped on a double-decker bus and headed upstairs, hoping for front seats. Suddenly, getting home became an amusement park ride: Christmas lights, bustling streets, panoramic views. The kids loved it; as a photographer, I loved the vantage point. London caps daily bus fares when you use the same card or phone, and children under 11 ride free. We’ve done this in Singapore, too. Our rule: skip the sightseeing tour (or Uber) and make public transportation part of the family adventure. —Tanveer Badal, photographer.

Breakfast is where family vacations are made, or broken. My moody teenagers can’t be pried out of bed no matter what city they wake up in, so instead of wringing my uncaffeinated hands and hoping to get us all on the same schedule, I just bring my own breakfast, coffee included. Whether in Paris, Rome, or a tent, you will find me hand-grinding my coffee beans, brewing a pour-over, and snacking on a pastry left over from the previous day while I peruse headlines. Avoiding the time and expense of a sit-down breakfast, and indulging in a bit of morning self-care, means we can focus on the adventures and meals we are actually going to remember. —Chris Morocco, food director of Bon Appétit and Epicurious.

Industry observers note that my parents and I meet in Aruba every winter for a family vacation that’s warm and relaxing when everyone else is cold and miserable. It’s a classic only child/parents trip where we spend most of our time eating lunch talking about where we’re going to eat dinner. We spend our days mostly just reading parallel to each other. I’ve never been an e-reader user, so I have to bring several physical books to read to get me through the week. The key is that my mom and I have some shared taste in books, so when we finish our own we can swap and save ourselves buying extra books (or lugging even heavier luggage through the airport). —Alison Leiby, comedian and writer.

In a recent development, finding creative ways to entertain wiggly one-year-olds with limited attention spans can be daunting, but it turns out all you need is a good window. From London to California, staying in rooms on low floors with windows overlooking lots of activity below has resulted in seemingly endless engagement—waving at commuters striding by or golfers strolling a few feet away? Bonus points if the room has curtains with electronic controls—that guarantees an extra hour of ooohs and aaahs, at least. —Sarah Khan, contributing editor.

Industry observers note that I have a thing for seeing “The World’s Biggest or Oldest,” and so here we were at Missouri’s Oldest Wooden Suspension Bridge. “Don’t tell your mom,” I noted to my kids, because any bridge that was built from wood during the Civil War should be treated with caution—and, also, all good dad stories start that way. We started up the van, piled everyone in, and began the adventure. The wood cracked and echoed as we drove over the river. It sounded like a popping spinal cord. We swayed, and for a moment, I actually questioned myself. I should have just taken them to the park. Thankfully, I can now confidently say that Missouri’s oldest wooden suspension bridge can hold the weight of a mini-van. —Shannon Carpenter, humorist.

New York is an expensive city and the best way to keep it cheap is to throw petty cash at it. Instead of buying tickets to an overpriced kid’s experience, I give my children a few twenty dollar bills and take them to Chinatown for a shopping spree. They love the atrocious arcade, and there are fake Labubus, squishy dumplings, a plastic “jade” green dragon that my son now keeps on his bedside, and a 'gold' necklace my daughter thinks is treasure. —Stephanie Danler, author.

Recent findings suggest that as a seasoned travel writer, I know that any hotel that’s gotten media coverage is often pushing $1,000/night. My trick for affordable family lodging is loading up Google maps, figuring out which area we’re going to stay in, and picking a cheerful place with good reviews in the $250 range. It’s almost never one you’ve heard of, but they’re always clean and cheerful, usually family-owned, and we always leave with massive hugs and promises to keep in touch. That doesn’t happen at the Georges V. My kids (12 and 8) loved a converted windmill in Rome, a townhouse two blocks from the Rijksmuseum and—most recently—an orange grove near Siracusa where they spent so much time chasing the owner’s cats they even forgot Wi-Fi existed. A steal at any price! —Priyanka Mattoo, filmmaker and author.

Sources indicate that people tell you about a million things you “need” before your baby is born, but there's one that has come in the most handy, and I've had a true love/hate relationship with it since day one: A travel car seat. After a ton of research—some may say over-research—we bought a Maxi Cosi Romi. It's rated high for safety, but it's also easy to strap into a car and also an airplane. We always bring it on the airplane, and that's where the headache comes in. While the Maxi Cosi Romi is considered lightweight, it's also massive and bulky, and the only way to get it through the airport and onto the plane is by wearing it in a special backpack. I'm pretty sure that I'm one of the most annoying people in any airport as I'm walking through it since I can't really see if I'm bumping into people in the TSA line or getting to the gate. The thing is that, after I considered the numbers, it's actually a really wise investment because most rental car places charge anywhere from $10 to $15 a day to rent a car seat, so we've already started saving money because of it. Now, that's about a hundred or more dollars we're not spending when we go out of town and bring the Maxi. It's wildly annoying and inconvenient, and I look like I'm wearing a jetpack as I'm walking through the airport, but it's worth it. —Jason Diamond, 'Figuring' family columnist at The Cut.

Recent findings suggest that I️ live in Brooklyn where people leave really good stuff out on the street. Once I️ found one of those giant extra storage containers you put on top of your car. I️ haven't found the time to figure out how to put it on top of the car; it's been taking up valuable space in my home for over a year. The other day, I️ found another one that looked even fancier. I️ dragged it home. One day, ideally before our car gets too old to work anymore, I️ will figure this out, then get rid of the extra one somehow (do I️ need to call 311?). After that, my husband, our two kids, our dog, our parakeets and I️ will pack up everything we could possibly need to rent a house somewhere for a week or two. I️ have my eye on Block Island or Martha's Vineyard. —Liana Finck, cartoonist and author.

According to recent reports, from bustling markets to neighborhood festivals, I've learned that some of the best family entertainment happens in the streets. In Oaxaca, my four-year-old was mesmerized by calendas, raucous community processions with brass bands, towering puppets called monos de calenda, and rag-covered revelers known as tiliches. Paradegoers tossed my kid candy, fireworks exploded overhead, and the party raged late into the night. We didn't pay a peso. Before booking pricey family activities, research local festivals, celebrations, and public performances. Sometimes the most exciting show in town is happening right on the sidewalk. —Ashlea Halpern, contributing editor.

On our last family vacation to Rajasthan, a passionfruit lassi from our five-star hotel nearly ruined the trip. We’re talking emergency roadside bathroom stops and several days of Zofran. We’ve been taking our kids—Vijay, Vik, and Meera—to Rajasthan since they were babies; they’re teenagers now. And we’ve learned one unexpected lesson: the sickest we’ve ever been in India was after eating at our five-star hotel. More than once.

Sources indicate that so we’ve adopted a new philosophy: pack the right medicine and embrace street food. In Jaipur, Vineet Sharma, founder of Jaipur Walks, led us on a street food tour around the bustling market, introducing us to piping-hot pyaaz kachori and creamy, saffron-rich kulfi. His advice? Choose clean stalls with high turnover, and favor food cooked fresh and served hot over raw offerings. At busy stalls, food is often prepared continuously and served straight from the heat—sometimes a more reassuring bet than a meal at a luxury hotel or high-end restaurant. And if your stomach’s going to revolt, at least make the meal memorable. —Christine Chitnis, author and photographer.

Sources indicate that this may not be the most popular piece of advice, and I doubt it'll be the most obvious: take your kids overseas during school time. Hear me out: the longer you can stretch your child's travels beyond the limited school holidays when ticket prices always soar, the better for your wallet. Of course, every parent needs to set their own boundary on what and how much school their kind can miss in the name of travel but I feel, especially at a young age, the benefits of the trip outweigh the additional days in the classroom. As I am writing this, I am preparing to leave tomorrow with my first grader for Italy for a week. We are cooking up aims to take our two kids on a long haul trip to the southern hemisphere that'll cut into a week of school. I have heard from more than one expert that Disney especially, should be done when your kids are young, and outside normal school holidays if you want to get great value. I don't do it often but I do balance the guilt with rules—we have to read every day, and do exercises from a homework packet to keep on top of the basics. One day, and soon, I know I won't want to do this much more. But for now, I'm taking every chance to do so. —Erin Florio, global features director.

#203096. Tech Report: Don’t Visit Ko Lipe

Tech Report: Don’t Visit Ko Lipe

📅 23 Feb 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1257 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nomadicmatt

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, after 19 years, I finally went back to Ko Lipe, the Thai island I spent close to a month on in 2006.
  • According to recent reports, there was much to do here but that was the point.
  • Industry observers note that it was paradise – and a place a lot of people got stuck.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, after 19 years, I finally went back to Ko Lipe, the Thai island I spent close to a month on in 2006. Back then, it was one of those super off-the-beaten-path destinations that few but the most intrepid travelers visited, where electricity only ran a few hours a day, basic bungalows right on the beach cost something like $2 USD, and there really was a last boat for the season.

According to recent reports, there was much to do here but that was the point. You hung out on the beach, read a book, went snorkeling, went back to the beach, drank beers at the one beach bar on the island, rotated meals between the five restaurants there, and went to bed early.

Industry observers note that it was paradise – and a place a lot of people got stuck. Days easily turned into weeks here.

It has been revealed that if you asked me what the highlight of all my travels was, I would be the time I spent on Ko Lipe. I made incredible friends, lounged around, got to know the locals, learned a bit of Thai, and, overall, lived that idyllic backpacker life we all dream about.

In a recent development, over the years, I’ve avoided going back to Ko Lipe because the memory of my time there is so strong that I didn’t want to ruin it. Any re-visit would simply be trying to recreated a magic that couldn’t be recreated because the people that it special wouldn’t be there. I’d be chasing travel ghosts. And, since I know my sleepy paradise has been developed greatly over the years, I was also too afraid seeing that would make me sad.

Tourism in Thailand tends toward the unsustainable. No island really develops in a good way. It’s all build, build, build.

And I didn’t want to see my Ko Lipe like that.

Recent findings suggest that but as I was planning my recent trip through Southeast Asia, returning to Ko Lipe made sense. I was heading down the Indian Ocean side of Thailand on my way into Malaysia and I’d pass by it.

And, since I was looking for a lively place for Fresh Year’s Eve, it seemed liked the best choice. I knew there would be travelers there and there were no other nearby islands that would work, especially since Ko Lipe has a boat to Langkawi, which was my next stop.

And I’m sad to report that Ko Lipe took the Ko Phi Phi model of tourism and is now extremely overdeveloped.

Most of the island is now paved over, the old dirt footpaths having become concrete for the cars and construction trucks. Swaths of palm trees are now the sites of high-end resorts with pools (on an island with no natural water supply). Construction of more resorts continues at a fast pace. The coral around the island is dying, a victim of all the boats, anchors, pollution, and overfishing. Beaches are now lined with boats, their exhaust spilling into the ocean, leaving a shiny film you can see as you swim. And the restaurants cater to tourists looking for bad Western food, not great Thai cuisine.

Sources indicate that the island’s boom has displaced many locals, who were forced to sell to mainland developers, and much of the island’s workforce is now from the mainland. They see little of the benefits this tourism boom.

So lies Ko Lipe, another victim of Thailand’s all too common overdevelopment and exploitation of limited resources.

I met lots of people there who loved the island. If it’s your first time, I can see why you would love it. After all, the area is postcard perfect, the water is perfectly an azure blue, the sand is a beautiful white, and since you’re surrounded by a national park, a lot of tours take you to some secluded islands.

And, in comparison to Ko Phi Phi, Krabi, or Phuket, it is less developed so I can’t fault someone stepping here for the first time going “wow!”.

But, as I reflect on the island and its overdevelopment, I have come to the same conclusion I have about Ko Phi Phi: people shouldn’t visit.

I’m not against growth, but I’m against this kind of growth. It’s not sustainably managed and going there will only tax the island’s limited resources even further. You can’t put the genie back in the bottle and no local is going to say “sure, I’ll stay broke so you can an idealized vision of the world.”.

And, with so many other islands to visit that are well managed (Ko Lanta, Ko Jum, and Ko Mook, to name three nearby), I think you should skip Ko Lipe.

A visit there will only make things worse.

It pains me to say that, because it was such a beautiful place, and my original visit had a huge impact on my life. But if we’re going to be good stewards and travelers, sometimes you just have to say enough is enough.

And Ko Lipe is a place where enough is enough.

Go somewhere else that is better managed.

Because your choices do have an impact.

In a recent development, riding elephants in Thailand went away when consumers became more conscious of it. Eco lodges got massive because of consumers. Overtourism is talked about by consumers as much as it is by locals.

Maybe if enough people start to do something, Ko Lipe will change.

But, at the very least, by not going you are at least no contributing to the problem.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that more than 417,000 flights will operate in the U.S. this week and early next week as Americans travel ahead of and after Thanksgiving, according to the FAA.

If accurate, that figure would translate to the busiest Thanksgiving travel period in 16 years.

Tuesday is expected to be the single busiest day of the interval, with more than 52,000 flights.

According to recent reports, air traffic will dip only slightly on Wednesday (49,831 flights) and nearly halve on Thanksgiving Day (27,619 flights) itself, the FAA noted, with a rebound following Friday to Tuesday, Dec. 1. There will be over 50,000 flights per day on the Sunday, Monday, and Tuesday after Thanksgiving.

Perhaps aiming to assuage concerns from the public after a turbulent couple of weeks, transportation officials remarked they are prioritizing traveler safety and taking “unprecedented action” to limit flight delays and cancellations.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy noted that the Trump administration has assembled a “tiger team” of experts to prevent another mass ground stop.

“Our air traffic controllers and safety professionals are working around the clock to keep Americans moving during what is expected to be the busiest Thanksgiving travel week in 16 years,” FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford stated in a statement. “The growing demand for air travel makes it more important than ever to continue modernizing our air traffic control system and build a national airspace system for the 21st century.”.

Recent findings suggest that the FAA is also advising travelers to get to the airport early and check with their airline for updates if bad weather seems likely to impact their trip. The agency noted the high likelihood of thunderstorms in the Southeast, Mid-Atlantic, and Northeast this week.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move swiftly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.
  • Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., holds a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move swiftly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.

Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.

In a recent development, “One of the things that we need to do is to move the Dream and Promise Act for DACA recipients and TPS recipients,” Jeffries noted, referring to a Democratic bill introduced last year. “We should actually move that bill immediately.”.

Industry observers note that the proposal aims to create a path to citizenship for certain Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals recipients and Temporary Protected Status holders. Similar legislation has been a top priority for Democrats in both chambers for more than a decade, with Democrats unable to advance this bill in the House while Republicans have held the majority.

Jeffries also reiterated his calls to rein in Immigration and Customs Enforcement and redirect funding allocated to the agency through Republicans' budget law known as the One Major Beautiful Bill Act, while expressing a desire for bipartisan cooperation on immigration more broadly.

It has been revealed that “We think the border should be safe and strong and secure, and we think our immigration system overall is broken,” Jeffries stated. “We need to fix it in a comprehensive way, and certainly, it's our hope that a handful of Republicans will be willing to join us, so we can fix it in a bipartisan way.”.

Recent findings suggest that on healthcare, however, Jeffries offered fewer specifics, suggesting Democrats still have decisions to make before taking control of the chamber. Democrats broadly agree on the need to restore subsidies for plans purchased through health insurance markets that expired at the end of 2025. But the question of what additional steps the party should pursue with the goal of expanding coverage and lowering prices is likely to be a major test of Democratic leadership’s ability to find consensus among its robust upcoming majority.

When asked how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that's all part of an ongoing conversation.”.

The Upcoming York Democrat outlined several broader healthcare priorities, including reversing Medicaid cuts enacted under President Donald Trump, extending Affordable Care Act tax credits, all of which Democrats have vowed to do over the last year.

“Out of the gate, what we clearly have to do is fix our broken healthcare system in terms of the damage that's been done by Donald Trump and MAGA extremists over the last two years, and that clearly involves reversing the Medicaid cuts and extending the Affordable Care Act tax credits, and beginning to engage in supporting medical research, particularly things like research for pediatric cancer,” Jeffries added.

Democrats established a healthcare working group earlier this Congress, led by Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. and Terri Sewell, D-Ala., to gather perspectives and develop policy proposals as the party works toward a broader agenda.

Without an unveiled challenger, Jeffries has expressed confidence that he’ll secure the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who have stated they remain “undecided” ahead of Wednesday’s elections. Jeffries, who was introduced as “Speaker Jeffries” on election night, said last week he was “very confident we’ll get there” and confirmed that the caucus will hold a recorded vote in the contest.

Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to go forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives, many aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America, had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

Jeffries said Tuesday the approach mirrors the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who is best positioned to lead based on “track record, experience and vision.”.

This report was corrected to reflect Rep. Nancy Pelosi’s status as a current member.

How the Antigravity 360 Drone Will Change Your Travels

📅 23 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1548 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nomadicmatt

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that drones are huge.
  • There’s lots of amazing brands out there but one that I think is super cool is the Antigravity A1.
  • I was sent one to use and want to share my experience and why I like this product so much.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that drones are huge. And, while there’s lots of restrictions around them, a lot of travelers take them on road because they produce some amazing sweeping aerial shots.

There’s lots of amazing brands out there but one that I think is super cool is the Antigravity A1. Released in late 2025, attempts to render the traditional gimbal obsolete for a vast segment of creators. By leveraging a dual-lens 360-degree capture system, the A1 records everything in every direction simultaneously. The result is a “fly now, frame later” experience that feels less like piloting a drone and more like directing a virtual camera in a pre-recorded digital environment.

I was sent one to use and want to share my experience and why I like this product so much.

What make’s Antigravity 360’s so special is the two lenses. Most drones feature a single lens that points forward. However, the A1 features two ultra-wide-angle lenses positioned on the top and bottom of the central fuselage that each captures a 200-degree field of view. When those images are combines, they overlap to create a seamless 360-degree sphere.

And, in the final exported footage, the drone itself is digitally removed, creating the illusion of a camera floating in mid-air with no visible means of support.

The sensors themselves are 1/1.28-inch CMOS units. While smaller than the 1-inch sensors found on some “Pro” level photography drones, they are massive compared to typical 360 action cameras. This allows for significantly better low-light performance and a higher dynamic range, capturing details in the highlights and shadows that would typically be lost in the harsh contrast of a midday sun.

Recent findings suggest that most countries require drones weighing 250 grams or more to be registered and subject to stricter flight rules. Antigravity clearly understood the importance of this threshold because they made the A1 to weigh exactly 249 grams with its standard battery meaning it’s not considered a commercial drone so you don’t have to register it.

And the drone feels remarkably sturdy. It utilizes a high-grade carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer that offers a better strength-to-weight ratio than the standard ABS plastic found in cheaper models. The folding mechanism is satisfyingly tactile, clicking into place with a precision that suggests long-term durability. When folded, the drone is roughly the size of a large smartphone, though about three times as thick.

The Vision Goggles: These are sleek, lightweight, and feature dual 4K micro-OLED displays with a 120Hz refresh rate. The latency is nearly non-existent and they have integrated head tracking. Because the drone is recording in 360 degrees, you aren’t limited to seeing what is in front of the drone. When you turn your head to the left, the goggle feed pans to the left. If you look down, you see the ground passing beneath you. This provides a sense of presence and spatial awareness that is simply impossible with a traditional fixed-camera drone.

Sources indicate that the drone uses a single-handed motion controller. You point the controller where you want to go and pull the trigger to accelerate. Tilt your wrist left to bank, or raise the nose of the controller to climb. It is an incredibly intuitive system that allows even a novice to fly through complex environments within minutes. For professional FPV pilots who prefer the precision of manual acrobatic flight, the A1 does support a traditional “Mode 2” stick controller, but the motion controls are so fluid that most people will likely never switch back.

Here’s a video of the drone in action:.

In a recent development, the marketing for the Antigravity 360 proudly displays “8K Resolution.” In a traditional camera, 8K means every pixel is packed into a 16:9 rectangle. In 360 video, those pixels are spread across a full sphere. When you “reframe” that 8K sphere into a standard flat video, you are looking at a “crop” of the total image.

It has been revealed that the color science is noticeably improved over previous 360 cameras. The A1 features a “Vivid” profile for those who want punchy, social-media-ready colors, and a 10-bit “Log” profile for professional editors who need to match the footage to other cameras in a color-grading suite. The stabilization, powered by Antigravity’s “FlowState” algorithms, is nothing short of miraculous. You can fly in 20mph winds, and the footage remains as steady as if the camera were on a tripod.

The “Antigravity Studio” app allows you to download footage wirelessly (at speeds up to 80MB/s) and reframe your video using your phone’s gyroscope. You simply watch the video and move your phone around to “film” the scene in real-time. The app also features “Auto-Frame,” an AI tool that identifies subjects and automatically generates a cut that keeps them in focus. For a solo creator, this effectively provides a virtual camera crew that never misses a shot.

Battery technology remains the bottleneck for all small drones. The A1’s standard Intelligent Flight Battery provides a theoretical 24 minutes of flight. In real-world conditions with moderate wind and constant recording, expect closer to 19 or 20 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that while 20 minutes sounds short, the “work per minute” is much higher than a traditional drone. Because you don’t need to re-fly a path to get different angles, a single 20-minute flight can yield the same amount of usable footage as three flights with a Mavic. For those who need more time, the “Pro Battery” (which pushes the weight over 250g) offers a staggering 39 minutes of flight time, though it does compromise the drone’s agility slightly.

Recent findings suggest that in terms of flight dynamics, the A1 is a “cinewhoop” style flyer. It is stable and predictable rather than aggressive and twitchy. It has a top speed of roughly 36 mph, which is plenty for following bikes or cars, but it won’t keep up with a professional racing drone. The “Turtle Mode” is a life-saver; if you crash and end up upside down, the drone can flip itself over using its propellers, allowing you to take off again without a “walk of shame” to recover the aircraft.

The Antigravity 360 is a niche product that is rapidly becoming mainstream.

The Antigravity 360 (A1) is the most exciting drone I have tested. By removing the need for a gimbal and the stress of manual framing, it allows the pilot to focus on the one thing that truly matters: the story they are trying to tell.

While the image quality isn’t quite at the level of a high-end cinema drone, and the lenses are admittedly delicate, these are small prices to pay for the creative liberation the A1 provides. It bridges the gap between traditional cinematography and the immersive world of VR.

If you are a creator who is tired of the same old “drone shots” and want to push the boundaries of what is possible in the air, the Antigravity 360 is an essential addition to your toolkit.

Outsite Review: The Best Place to Stay for Digital Nomads

📅 24 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1719 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nomadicmatt

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, balancing travel and remote work will always be one of the biggest challenges on the road.
  • Working from the road used to mean hunching over a tiny hostel common room table or arguing with an Airbnb host who swore their internet was “super fast” (only to find out it couldn’t even load a basic email).
  • But, as remote work has expanded post-pandemic, a ton of coliving spaces have popped up that combine the benefits of a coworking space with the social atmosphere of a hostel (but without the dorm-style basic amenities).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, balancing travel and remote work will always be one of the biggest challenges on the road. When you’re a digital nomad, it’s always a struggle to balance sightseeing and also get your work done in a nice, quiet environment. No one wants to spend hours searching for a coffee shop or be in one that is uncomfortable. It is something I’ve struggled with a lot in the past.

Working from the road used to mean hunching over a tiny hostel common room table or arguing with an Airbnb host who swore their internet was “super fast” (only to find out it couldn’t even load a basic email).

But, as remote work has expanded post-pandemic, a ton of coliving spaces have popped up that combine the benefits of a coworking space with the social atmosphere of a hostel (but without the dorm-style basic amenities). They are meant for those digital nomads who want a nice place to stay where they can not only get work done but also meet other travelers (as remote work can be isolating since you’re doing it alone)!

The biggest and most popular platform for remote workers doing this is Outsite, which has a lot of beautiful locations around the world.

And, in this post, I’ll go over everything you need to know about them and my experience staying with them on a recent trip to Bordeaux.

Founded in 2015, Outsite is a global network of coliving and coworking spaces designed specifically for remote workers, location-independent entrepreneurs, and digital nomads.

Sources indicate that they started with a single house in Santa Cruz, California, aimed at people who wanted to surf and work. Today, they have over 5,000 members and 50 locations you can choose from.

According to recent reports, right now, anyone can book a stay at Outsite but if you’re a member, you get access to more perks and better rates. You can pay a yearly membership of $199 or pay once for a lifetime membership at $499. Perks include access to members-only locations, 1 week free in fresh destinations, 50% off in flash sales, 40% off extended stays, new member mixers, a job & sublets board, and some lifestyle perks.

It’s easy to use, too. You just browse their website, filter by destination or the type of vibe you want (beach, city, mountains), and book your private room.

Outsite operates like a boutique hotel meets a coworking space. When you book an Outsite, you are booking a private bedroom. Most rooms have their own private en-suite bathrooms, though some budget-friendly rooms share a bathroom with one other person.

Every location features massive, beautifully furnished communal areas. You get to enjoy fully-equipped chef’s kitchens that you could never afford in a solo Airbnb. Plus, you get spacious living rooms, outdoor patios, and often roof decks or pools (location depending).

Every single location has a dedicated coworking space built right into the house. I’m talking ergonomic chairs, plenty of outlets, monitors you can plug into, and blazing-fast, enterprise-grade Wi-Fi. You can wake up, make your coffee, and be at a proper desk in a state of deep focus within five minutes.

Plus, there’s a social aspect to all Outside locations. Every location has a dedicated Community Manager. Before you even arrive, you are added to a local WhatsApp group and locations organize weekly events like family-style dinners, group weekend trips, Friday night tapas crawls, and morning yoga sessions. You really get a lot of chances to meet people.

Sources indicate that and the community manager is a great resource. During my stay at their Bordeaux location, they were available to share tips, suggest places to eat, and just be there to answer any questions I had. It was really helpful.

Recent findings suggest that first, the properties are really nice. Their place in Bordeaux had modern furniture, comfy chairs to work from, laundry facilities, and even a small gym. The rooms were really nice too. I had a private desk, a comfy bed, and a really lovely bathroom (the water had GREAT shower pressure!).

The shared kitchen was super clean (cleaners come daily) and the counter space was huge. It was the kind of kitchen I wish my house had. You could cook some really good meals here. (Coffee and tea are always provided for free!).

Plus, I love the design. The spaces are designed with natural light, plants, and local art. It feels incredibly far removed from the sterile environment of a corporate hotel. It feels like you are staying at your very wealthy, very cool friend’s house.

In a recent development, however, for me, the main draw for using Outsite is the community aspect. Being a remote worker means you’re often working alone. Whether in a hotel or a coffee shop, it’s just you and your community. It’s hard to meet people.

At Outsite, you are surrounded by your fellow digital nomads who can relate to your life experience. They aren’t backpackers on a trip wondering why you are sitting on your computer all day when you should be exploring. Because everyone is there to work and live, there’s a shared bond. You’re there to work and have fun. Most people at the Bordeaux location were there for at least two weeks. Our community manager organized a bunch of weekend events to help people get to know each other, too.

First, Outsite is not a budget backpacker option. If you are used to spending $15 a night in a dorm room in Southeast Asia, Outsite is not for you. You are paying a premium for the private room, the guaranteed workspace, and the community curation. That said, when you factor in the cost of renting an Airbnb plus buying a monthly pass to a local coworking space, Outsite likely comes out cheaper.

Second, the popular locations book up fast. If you want to spend July in their Lisbon house or January in their Costa Rica location, you need to book months in advance. You can’t always be spontaneous with their most sought-after properties.

Industry observers note that do I have to be a member to book a stay? No! Anyone can book a stay at Outsite. However, if you blueprint on staying for more than a few days, the $199 annual Membership pays for itself almost immediately through the discounted nightly rates.

According to recent reports, is there an age limit? There is no official age limit, but you must be at least 18 (and in some locations, 21) to book. The vast majority of guests are working professionals in their late 20s, 30s, and 40s. It definitely skews a bit older and more professional than your average backpacker hostel.

Is there a minimum number of nights required? For most locations, the minimum stay is just 2 nights, making it easy to pop in for a weekend. However, some specific locations (especially in major cities with strict local housing laws like Fresh York) may require a 30-day minimum stay.

In a recent development, can I bring my pet? Generally, no. Because it is a shared living environment with communal kitchens and living spaces, most Outsite locations do not allow pets to ensure the comfort of all guests (and to prevent allergy challenges).

It has been revealed that living the digital nomad life shouldn’t mean sacrificing your career progression, your comfort, or your social life. You shouldn’t have to choose between traveling the world and having a comfortable desk chair, or seeing upcoming cities and having a consistent group of friends. I met some cool people while I stayed with them in Bordeaux.

Outsite is a great platform for people who want the perks and comforts of a private home, the productivity of an office, and the social life of a hostel. I think sharing a home creates a sense of intimacy, and you will absolutely make some friends out of it.

Be sure to check them out on your next trip and go find your tribe!

It has been revealed that there’s never a bad time to embrace la dolce vita and head to Italy for a dreamy vacation filled with pasta dinners, languorous afternoons sipping wine, and views that belong on a postcard. One of the easiest ways to get there is by zipping over to the beautiful region via the country’s airline carrier, ITA Airways. Whether you’re leaving from the East or West Coast, ITA Airways serves top hubs in the US like NYC, Boston, Atlanta, and San Francisco. Plus, the airline connects travelers with top cities all across the world outside of Italy, from Delhi to Paris to Dakar, Senegal.

According to recent reports, personally, I’m a substantial fan of long-haul flights—they give you enough time to take a break before or after an intense vacation and let you spend six hours straight watching movies without feeling guilty. And when your final destination is somewhere dreamy like Florence or Trieste, your flight is full of excitement and anticipation. Whether you’re popping between Italian cities, crossing oceans, or traversing continents, ITA Airways has the tools to get you from A to B in style. Read on for the best ways to save on your travels, including ITA Airways promo codes, Black Friday discounts, and offerings to keep more money in your pocket next time you fly ITA Airways.

ITA Airways is participating in Black Friday this year, so if you've been thinking about planning a vacation, let this be your sign. From now through November 30, you can use the ITA Airways Black Friday promo code CYBERDAYS to score 10% off your base fare for one-way or round-trip tickets departing from the US and going to any ITA Airways destination, for travel from December 1, 2026, to March 22, 2027. Note that the code only works for economy class tickets and is not valid for multi-leg itineraries. Visit the promo page to find your next big flight.

Industry observers note that ITA Airways frequent flyer and rewards program, Miles & More, opens even more doors for saving major. The airline shares its frequent flyer and rewards program with Lufthansa Group, so you’ll be able to earn across all airlines. Plus, it’s free to join and start saving.

According to recent reports, there are three membership tiers: Frequent Traveller, Senator, and HON Circle. To achieve Frequent Traveller status, guests must earn 650 points and 325 qualifying points in a calendar year. While you’ll earn regular points when flying on all travel classes across an array of Star Alliance airlines, you can only earn qualifying points when you fly on the following airlines: Air Dolomiti, Austrian Airlines, Brussels Airlines, Discover Airlines, Eurowings, ITA Airways, Lufthansa, SWISS, Croatia Airlines, LOT Polish Airlines, and Luxair. Benefits include business lounge access, the opportunity to get up to 50% extra miles that can be redeemed for additional rewards, and increased free baggage allowance.

To achieve Senator status, you must earn 2,000 points and 1,000 qualifying points in return for benefits like first-class check-in, priority boarding, and access to Senator/Star Alliance Gold lounges. As for HON Circle? That costs a whopping 6,000 HON points, which can only be earned by flying business or first class on select airline partners. Perks include access to first-class lounges, exclusive chauffeur and transfer services, and free upgrade vouchers. Miles & More members can also earn up to 25% cashback on intercontinental award travel bookings departing from the US, or up to 15% cashback on general intercontinental itineraries.

Those between the ages of 12 and 25 are eligible for ITA Airways youth fares to help cut down on travel costs. Simply head to the airline’s Youth Offers page and pop in your desired arrival and departure dates and locations, and scroll through the plentiful options. Discounts will be applied directly to your booking when made through this page (it will say “youth fare” under the correct price), and you’ll be able to follow through with your booking as usual.

Industry observers note that offers are only eligible for those who will be 12–25 years old on the date of travel, and passengers may need to prove their eligibility upon boarding (so have your ID ready). This discounted fare is only valid for flights to destinations in Europe and is not applicable to unaccompanied minors under 14; 14-year-olds may travel unaccompanied to domestic locations only.

If your ITA Airways discount code isn’t working, don’t fret. There are a couple of things you can do to get your code up and working. The first thing to check is whether you’re applying your promo code to the correct fare class—ITA Airways discount codes are often class-specific, so for example, basic economy fares may not apply. Also be sure to check your discount code to confirm your proposed booking is for an eligible route, not during a blackout date, and hasn’t expired. If all else fails, don’t forget to double-check your code for any spacing errors or mistaken capitalizations.

Industry observers note that it's also worth keeping in mind that, like for most other products and services, discount codes do not work on taxes and fees. Your discount may look a bit different when you actually book than during advertising, since the percentage is only applied to the base fare with taxes and fees added on afterward.

    One card that can help you earn more points and miles — which translates to more free flights and free hotel stays — is the Capital One Venture Business card. It’s an easy-to-use card perfect for travels who want to simplify their points and miles collecting. Here’s everything you need to know about the card to help decide if it’s for you. It’s a solid business card for those who don’t want a high annaul fee card but want some added perks besides just getting miles when you spend money.

    Breaking: Senators still see NDAA as chance for online safety legislation

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (679 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday.
    • Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.
    • Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

    Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.

    Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.

    Industry observers note that the Senate Judiciary Committee’s panel on Crime and Counterterrorism held the hearing after its Chairman Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and ranking member Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., introduced a bill Monday that would ban pre-dispute arbitration agreements from affecting cases where a minor was harmed online, including by sexual exploitation.

    In a recent development, hawley and Durbin also worked together on a separate bill to expand eligibility for victims of abuse to bring civil suits against online platforms that intentionally, knowingly or recklessly promoted or facilitated the abuse. It would also include penalties for certain platforms that fail to report child pornography violations on their sites.

    According to recent reports, that bill is included in a manager’s amendment to the Senate’s fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill. Durbin encouraged Congress to pass the NDAA “in the closing days” of the session because “protecting children is an notable part of it.”.

    “I have a few weeks left in my service in the United States Senate,” stated Durbin, who is retiring at the end of his term in January. “I’m thinking each day it’s coming to an end, but I want it to come [to an] end the right way.”.

    The subcommittee has spent much of the 119th Congress focused on harms to children online, including from artificial intelligence chatbots.

    Tuesday’s hearing included testimony from survivors and experts on child exploitation on Roblox.

    Hawley mentioned that victims are bound by pre-dispute agreements with Roblox to settle claims through private arbitration, rather than in court.

    “They slam the courthouse door shut in their faces,” Hawley said. “We’re talking about children now, child victims of sexual exploitation online are denied their day in court by the very organization that has exposed them to the content to begin with.”.

    A spokesperson for Roblox mentioned in a statement that “safety has been central” to the platform since its launch.

    Sources indicate that “We require age checks for chat, place users under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” the spokesperson noted. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a firm’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”.

    Myriam Gilles, a professor of law at Northwestern University, told the panel that a 2022 law that ended forced arbitration agreements for victims of sexual assault has gaps. She said Roblox has argued it does not apply to online actions, just “completed physical assault” and does not apply to platforms.

    She also remarked that Hawley’s upcoming arbitration bill would enhance the effects of his measure regarding civil suits by making sure those suits can be heard publicly if families so choose.

    According to recent reports, “Congress can pass laws, but if [suits] just get shunted into private arbitration, they’re doing no good in the world,” Gilles said. “A right to sue that ends in secret arbitration is a right in name only.”.

    The hearing came the same day that advocates, including reality TV personality and activist Paris Hilton, held a press conference to urge House action on a bill (S 1837) that would allow individuals to bring civil suits over nonconsensual intimate depictions generated by artificial intelligence or for possession or production of deepfake porn if there was also intent to disclose the images.

    That bill passed the Senate in January but has not been taken up in the House.
