    #203069. 19 Best Resorts in California, From Pebble Beach to Napa Valley

    📅 07 Aug 2020 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (3044 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    19 Best Resorts in California, From Pebble Beach to Napa Valley

    📅 07 Aug 2020 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3044 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In the late 1800s, travelers arriving on the West Coast found that the gold rush had dried up, but another kind of treasure was waiting in its wake: the health spa.
    • Sources indicate that of course, it’s a big state with hundreds of different landscapes, so finding the right resort is all about knowing what makes you come alive.
    • Auberge Collection’s third property in Napa Valley is set on a historic Wine Country ranch founded in 1856 by Judge Edward Stanly.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In the late 1800s, travelers arriving on the West Coast found that the gold rush had dried up, but another kind of treasure was waiting in its wake: the health spa. Soon, doctors back east were prescribing trips to the Golden State for ailing patients in search of restorative sunshine, mineral springs, and fresh air. California’s reputation as a destination for serious R&R has persisted ever since. From beachfront properties in SoCal to redwood hideaways along the Massive Sur coast to vineyardside estates in Napa Valley, the best resorts in California are a kind of gold standard all their own.

    Sources indicate that of course, it’s a big state with hundreds of different landscapes, so finding the right resort is all about knowing what makes you come alive. Looking to spend time on the links? There are legendary fairways waiting at Pebble Beach. Craving an off-the-grid escape? Decamp to a secluded sanctuary in the Santa Rosa Mountains. Prefer five-star amenities with near-clairvoyant service, or a home base for wine tastings and lavish dining? Consider it covered. Read on for the best resorts in California, where the good life is the real gold rush.

    Auberge Collection’s third property in Napa Valley is set on a historic Wine Country ranch founded in 1856 by Judge Edward Stanly. Guests can choose from 135 cottages, rooms, and suites—decorated in oatmeal and beige hues with leather and oak furnishings—all with private terraces and outdoor showers. Standout amenities include Guatemalan heated robes, yoga mats, and Theragun massage tools. Bay Area food lovers make the trek here just to sample chef Anthony Stagnaro’s ingredient-focused meals at the resort’s Avroko-designed restaurant, Bear; others prefer to sip rosé at the French countryside-inspired Basin Bar or order a scoop of ice cream at The Window. But don’t expect to drink wine all day: This wellness-focused resort can curate fitness optimization programs, send you out on a cycling adventure with a pro, or arrange a hot-air balloon ride for the whole family. —Jen Murphy.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Industry observers note that while it’s tempting to paint Sonoma as a sleepy sweep of California Wine Country, the truth is, the county is every bit as—if not more—booming than neighboring Napa. It’s got Michelin-starred restaurants, shiny upcoming tasting rooms, and major-name hotels cropping up on the regular. But to try a little of that sweet Sonoma of yesteryear, there’s no better place than Farmhouse Inn. Located near the Russian River—and within easy driving distance to charming Healdsburg, as well as some of the region's best vineyards—this 25-room property feels delightfully laid-back and intimate. The Inn has five different room categories, all with a country-chic look; bright and airy with white wainscoting, pillowy bedding, and haute-rustic touches that might include a personal welcome message on a small blackboard, a fireplace, and comfortable overstuffed chairs. The Farmhouse Restaurant occupies a beautiful space and offers an ever-evolving chef’s tasting menu with hyper-local ingredients paired with, naturally, a stellar regional wine list. All in all, Farmhouse Inn looks and feels like a classic New England country charmer—with California Wine Country street cred. —Rebecca Misner.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    This outstanding Napa Valley hotel is set on 33 acres of vineyards and olive groves—needless to say, the views are spectacular. Sumptuous cottages done in sun and earth tones have wood-burning fireplaces and refrigerators stocked with local wines and cheeses; bathrooms come with skylights and flat-screen TVs. The restaurant serves Wine Country cuisine with French and Mediterranean influences, and its terrace has heaters for dining out on cool evenings. Enjoy Italian ices and chilled towels at the pool and Reiki at La Pagode, an Asian-style pavilion. —Todd Plummer.

    Napa has a handful of excellent hotels and no shortage of fabulous wineries and tasting rooms, but this is the first full-on luxury resort that marries the two. The property’s 85 rooms and suites, as well as 20 private residences, are surrounded by acres of vineyards. The bar and dining space are gorgeous—soaring ceilings, a glassed-in kitchen, and a wall of glass doors that open onto a huge terrace with a firepit—but made cozy by comfy booths and warm lighting. The on-site winery and its tasting room are another way this resort stands out. It’s a dream to walk from your room to a tasting and not have to worry about driving or calling a car. —R.M.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Industry observers note that northern California’s Wine Country retreats often model themselves on faraway places; destinations with longer traditions and more old-world gravitas. This is too bad, because their location, between the Pacific and the Mayacamas Mountains, is pure magic, and by this point on the domestic wine timeline, there’s no need to apologize for who you are. This is why the arrival of Montage’s first property in the region, and Sonoma’s first large-scale luxury resort, was so exciting when it opened in 2020. It celebrates its own landscape, leaving the 22,000 live oaks in place and pulling a palette of dun and moss from the surrounding sun-soaked vineyards. The restaurant offers a bounty of Sonoma’s best, with everything—from the Pliny the Elder IPA to the lamb shank—sourced from within miles. And the local sixth-generation vintners who frequent the sprawling patio bar are happy to remind you that there is, in fact, plenty of history in these parts. —R.M.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    According to recent reports, there are golf resorts, and then there’s Casa Palmero at Pebble Beach. The course, Pebble Beach Golf Links, opened more than 100 years ago in 1919, and has enjoyed as long and storied a history as any. The resort, a former private residence that opened in 1999, is directly on the course—rooms overlook the first and second fairways—making it an absolute dream for golfers. But Casa Palmero offers so much more than tee times. The rooms have a countryside vibe—spacious with wood-burning fireplaces, exposed ceiling beams, and wrought-iron fixtures—while the Spa at Pebble Beach offers award-winning service. Plus, it’s only a five-minute walk down to the peaceful beach.

    Set on 500 acres in the foothills of the Santa Lucia Mountains along California’s Central Coast, Carmel Valley Ranch is located just shy of 13 miles from the Monterey Bay Aquarium and historic Cannery Row. At check-in, you’ll receive a list of the resort’s scheduled activities, and staff will likely share their favorites—and you should pay attention. Options range from guided hikes and yoga to archery lessons and picnics with Pablo and Paco, a pair of resident miniature donkeys. There are also multiple pools, tennis and pickleball courts, and an 18-hole Pete Dye–designed golf course. If the blinds are up at the on-site creamery, stopping by the window to watch the cheesemaker in action is a must. Along with chickens and a salt house, the organic garden is home to veggies, flowers, and honeybees. Menus at signature restaurant Valley Kitchen showcase fresh, local ingredients—many of which are grown or produced on the resort. —Dana Rebmann.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    This beloved Substantial Sur resort, which dramatically overlooks the Pacific and is surrounded by acres of forest, received a total reboot in 2025. And while it may look newly introduced—rooms have all been updated with plenty of wood and neutrals, 15 luxe safari-style tents have been added to the roster, and the spa got a relaxation deck that looks out at the ocean—it hasn't lost its laid-back 1970s vibe. It's still, hands down, one of the most magical places to disconnect and get back in touch with nature. —Christina Ohly Evans.

    In a recent development, the Post Ranch Inn is a total immersion in the singular landscape of Significant Sur, in environs defined by a sense of understated luxury. The Ranch’s 40 rooms have all been designed to both blend in with and have a light touch upon the land, and range from tree houses to clifftop suites with expansive views of the mountains to the east or, better yet, the ocean’s expanse to the west. Engage with the environment some more by exploring the property’s hiking trails, taking a tour of the chef’s garden, or signing up for a falconry lesson. —Lauren Sloss.

    Check Availability at Hotels.com.

    It might seem like a mistake to go to Santa Barbara and not stay close to the shore, but the moment you make the turn inland onto San Ysidro Road, you realize that being here isn’t about visiting Santa Barbara; it’s about visiting the ranch. Just 38 cottages, each with its own unique layout, decor, and view, are spread out over 550 acres, but rather than being scattered, they form a ring within the property. At the resort’s center is a collection of gardens as well as a rectangular pool that overlooks the canyon. Some of the curated finds you’ll see throughout are museum-quality art, antiques sourced from the owner’s world travels, and handmade wallpapers. But San Ysidro Ranch isn’t your typical hotel—as its history of having legendary guests like Jacqueline and John F. Kennedy, who honeymooned here, or John Huston, who finished writing the screenplay for The African Queen on the property, can attest. It continues its legacy as a celebrity refuge, as modern-day A-listers use this tucked-away spot to truly hide out and escape—which is what you should do too. —Samantha Brooks.

    This is the original Hollywood hideaway with seven acres of land nestled in the foothills of the American Riviera. At El Encanto, you’ll have views overlooking the Pacific Coast with the rose-colored mountains rising behind you. The property has 90 rooms, but it never feels crowded; in fact, it feels private and idyllic. It has a fantastic luxe Spanish colonial charm without being annoying or precious. Whether you’re hiding away in a lush garden suite with a fireplace and a patio or just swanning around on the terrace for an alfresco farmers market lunch, it feels just right: low-key but ultra stylish. Call it what it is: a retreat. —Daniel Scheffler.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Sources indicate that arriving at Rosewood Miramar Beach, with its military-straight rows of white roses and pristine clapboard cottages, feels like landing on a postcard-perfect street in Cape Cod. If it all seems a little too perfect, well, there was time to get things right. The former Miramar by the Sea Hotel occupied these 16 oceanfront acres from 1889 until it closed for renovations in 2000. The hotel sat half-demolished for years, its second act tangled in red tape. It took SoCal billionaire developer Rick Caruso and the Hong Kong–based Rosewood Hotel Group to push the project through. And while it may have been tempting to scrap the past after such a treacherous road to reopening, the new Miramar deliberately throws back. Lemon-yellow-and-white striped umbrellas flank a rectangular pool where the Scoop Shop serves up fountain drinks, ice cream cones, and burgers. Overlooking the ocean, there’s Caruso’s, the type of place where you order a martini with your cacio e pepe alongside a heaping dollop of la dolce vita (the chef hails from Harry’s Bar in Rome)—and, in a state where “formal flip-flops" are a thing, one that blessedly enforces a dress code. In case you start to feel too lost in the 1950s, an outpost from Malibu Farm and a Goop boutique remind you that this is indeed modern-day Cali. —R.M.

    Check Availability at Hotels.com.

    According to recent reports, time slows down as you drive down the oversized, oak-tree-lined driveway at Alisal Ranch. Immediately upon checking in, you're greeted with countryside hospitality that makes you feel like you're light-years away from LA. The rooms are furnished with just the right amount of country Western kitsch, complete with wood-burning fireplaces, Pendleton blankets, and vintage paintings, and the beds are incredibly comfy—the perfect spot to rest your head after a day of adventuring. The highlight of your weekend will undoubtedly be horseback riding through groves of oaks up to the pancake breakfast. And the bar deserves a nod too, with a giant fireplace that makes for the perfect spot to enjoy a whiskey neat. —K.S.

    Check Availability at Hotels.com.

    In a recent development, to book a stay at this impeccably designed escape, guests must send an inquiry through the website—a sign of just how exclusive the hotel is. The reward is an extremely private getaway with a relaxing, neutral design and an incredible Nobu restaurant. Opened in April 2017, this serene escape was once a 1950s-era beach motel. Now, it's a study in high-design restraint—which is clear after setting one foot inside its almost hidden entrance. Guests enter through a courtyard that looks out onto the ocean, which leads to a beautiful garden. Follow the path to a deck made from ipe wood that overlooks Carbon Beach and Malibu Pier. —Brooke Porter Katz.

    Check Availability at Tripadvisor.

    Montage Laguna Beach is a polished, residential-style resort set on 30 oceanfront acres along one of Southern California’s most scenic stretches of coastline. Opened in 2003 as the brand’s flagship, the hotel continues to deliver consistent high-level service, a strong food and beverage program, and a true sense of privacy despite its size. Every one of the 263 rooms has an ocean view and outdoor space, and the property's layout, from the cliffside paths, tiered lawns, and access to Treasure Island Beach, makes it easy to settle in and stay awhile. Guests skew toward special-occasion travelers, West Coast couples, families, and loyal Montage regulars who return year after year. Highlights include the 20,000-square-foot Spa Montage, the renovated Mosaic Pool, direct beach access, and the return of Studio Mediterranean, the resort’s stellar fine-dining venue. While there’s no tennis or golf on-site, the concierge can arrange access at a nearby club. —Michelle Gross.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Sources indicate that time seems to slow down as you pull up to this sprawling Spanish revival hotel. Birds chirp from atop the towering oak trees, and the peaceful running fountains set the tone for a zen-like serenity that'll carry through your weekend. The rooms are personal retreats, many with soaking tubs, hand-painted Spanish tile, gold-auburn granite, and cobalt blue accents that give a modern Mediterranean look. Some rooms even have stucco fireplaces with seating, the perfect spot to tuck into a book and indulge in the rejuvenating spirit of Ojai. If that's not enough for you, the pools here are worth the visit alone—attentive staff, killer views, and plenty of space to hop around to keep the scenery fresh. —Krista Simmons.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    It has been revealed that toeing the line between self-improvement sabbatical and bona fide vacation, Sensei Porcupine Creek is the ideal getaway for the chronic over-achiever: a place where real R&R is achieved proactively, through science and strategy, and in utter seclusion. Formerly the private estate of tech wizard and Silicon Valley billionaire Larry Ellison, Sensei’s co-founder, this intensely isolated retreat hidden in the foothills of the Santa Rosa Mountains is the second outpost for Sensei, and it marked the brand’s debut in the continental United States. (Its first, Sensei Lānaʻi, A Four Seasons Resort, opened in 2019.) But it’s also the brand’s first true standalone property, and with a lush, 75-acre golf course, a glamorous lagoon-style pool, and tennis facilities modeled after those at the nearby Indian Wells Tennis Garden—which hosts the annual BNP Paribas Tennis Tournament—it really does stand alone. —Betsy Blumenthal.

    The Resort at Pelican Hill, located in the ultra-exclusive Newport Coast zip code, has a luxurious Tuscan vibe, with well-manicured hills overlooking the Pacific, beautiful villas and bungalows, and Roman aqueduct–style architecture. At 504 acres, it's huge—so huge that you'll likely need your car to get to your room. It's also surrounded by 50,000 acres of protected green spaces. You'll want to leave plenty of time to relax by the Coliseum Pool, the resort's crown jewel. —Archana Ram.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    This sprawling getaway is peak California. Think orange groves, bright pink bougainvillea, and Spanish Colonial architecture. The main features—the suites, restaurants, lobby—are spread out across 45 acres, making it feel more like a luxurious neighborhood than a typical resort. Located in Rancho Santa Fe, a ritzy enclave 25 miles north of downtown San Diego, this place has the whole package—beautiful decor, dedicated service, next-level amenities, well-manicured grounds, and a serene vibe. —Jennie Nunn.

    Check Availability at Mr and Mrs Smith.

    What is the best luxury resort in California?

    San Ysidro Ranch, at the foot of the Santa Ynez Mountains, is one of the best resorts in the world, let alone California. The property sprawls across 550 acres of citrus groves, gardens, and hiking trails, and each of its 38 rooms is a luxury cottage with a stone fireplace and antique furnishings that reflect its 130+ year history. Dignitaries like Winston Churchill, Audrey Hepburn, and Lucille Ball have stayed here—not to mention JFK and Jackie Kennedy, who called it their honeymoon hotel in 1953.

    What is the best place to visit in California if you're a first-time visitor?

    It has been revealed that california is so varied that it’s hard to pick a favorite zone, but there are few places in the world like Major Sur, where redwoods tower overhead and dramatic cliffs drop to the Pacific below. It can be a bit rustic, but that’s a big part of the charm.

    What is the difference between a hotel and resort?

    A hotel is mainly a place to sleep. A resort is the destination itself. Resorts typically sit on larger grounds and bundle the amenities you’d otherwise have to leave to find, like spas, pools, golf, multiple restaurants, and organized activities, so you can spend your whole stay on-property. In California, that might mean a round of golf at Pebble Beach before dinner, or a day of hiking, a massage, and a wine tasting without needing to hop in your car.

    How we choose the best resorts in California.

    Every hotel review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind.

    Traveling can be a noisy affair—from crying babies on airplanes to busy main streets with honking cars that drive past your hotel room at 3 a.m. While the noises of a fresh city can certainly be worth experiencing (whether that be actual music rooted in a specific location or the ambient sounds of church bells and passing trolleys), not all sounds are made the same. To help you block out any unnecessary background noise and get a good night’s sleep—or simply a moment of peace and quiet—Loop earplugs come in handy. Nothing will run you down quite as promptly while on vacation as poor sleep and no relaxation.

    According to recent reports, as a personal favorite earplug of mine, I can attest that Loops are the ideal travel companion, whether that be for getting some shut-eye on the plane, helping you focus on remote work in a crowded coffee shop, or protecting your eardrums at a club in Lisbon. Read on to see how you can save money on a pair for yourself with Loop Earplugs discount codes this Black Friday.

    Loop has nine different styles depending on your needs, ranging from a heavier-duty noise-dampening experience ideal for a night of deep sleep to the perfect buds to protect your ears during a concert or music festival. The products range slightly in style and how much noise they filter so you can create a personalized experience to match your needs.

    Mary Peltola unseats Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (771 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Mary Peltola speaks during her election night party in Anchorage on Nov.
    • In a recent development, former Rep.
    • The Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Former Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola speaks during her election night party in Anchorage on Nov. 3. (Charly Triballeau/ AFP via Getty Images).

    In a recent development, former Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, giving Senate Democrats their ninth pickup of the midterm elections and bringing their caucus’s total seats in the next Congress to 56.

    The Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday, a full two weeks after Election Day. The latest tranche of ballots counted put the former congresswoman past the 50-percent threshold to win the election outright without Alaska’s ranked choice voting system kicking in.

    With her victory, Peltola, who is Yup’ik, becomes one of the first Native American women elected to the Senate, along with fellow Democrat Peggy Flanagan, who won the open seat in Minnesota this month.

    “As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first.,” Peltola stated in a statement after the race was called.

    Industry observers note that the Alaska race was the final Senate contest to be called in a midterm election that saw Democrats win commanding majorities in both chambers of Congress. Besides Alaska, Democrats also flipped Senate seats in North Carolina, Maine, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi.

    Industry observers note that peltola, a former state legislator, made history in 2022 when she became the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, winning a special election for the state’s at-large district. She comfortably won the general election that fall but was narrowly unseated in 2024 by Republican Nick Begich.

    She entered the Senate contest in January, positioning herself as an independent-minded Democrat and invoking the legacies of two well-liked Alaska Republicans, the late Sen. Ted Stevens and the late Rep. Don Young, whom she succeeded in the House.

    She campaigned on the slogan “fish, family, freedom” and played up her moderate views and deep roots in the state.

    But the race was marked by allegations of political gamesmanship. In addition to the incumbent Sullivan, a retired colonel in the U.S. Marine Corps Reserves, the Senate ballot also included a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan. The New York Times reported late last month that operatives aligned with Peltola’s campaign were involved in the effort to recruit the second Dan Sullivan in an attempt to confuse voters.

    Peltola has said she had no connection to the scheme.

    Prior to Election Day, the Trump administration filed a lawsuit seeking to delay certification of the result if Sen. Sullivan were to lose. The lawsuit was tossed earlier this month by a federal judge.

    Recent findings suggest that trump also suggested that all votes cast for Dan J. Sullivan should be added to the incumbent’s total. “If you add them up, Dan Sullivan wins,” the president told reporters Monday. But as of Tuesday evening when the race was called, Peltola had more votes than both Sullivans combined.

    The Alaska race was initially viewed as a long shot for Democrats. The Last Frontier has elected a Democratic senator just once in the past 50 years – in 2008, when Mark Begich ousted Stevens. Begich, the Democratic uncle of the current Republican congressman, served a single term before he was ousted by Sullivan in 2014.

    But anger in Alaska over the rising cost of food and fuel — already among the highest in the nation — provided Democrats with an opening.

    Recent findings suggest that "56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago," Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer said in a statement Tuesday night. "But I knew if we concentrated on getting the best candidates, and if we focused like a laser on the costs, corruption, and chaos that Donald Trump has wrought throughout America, we would have shot.".

    In other Alaska races, Democrats flipped the governor’s mansion, with former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins winning an open-seat race to become the first Democrat elected governor of the state since Tony Knowles won a second term in 1998.

    In a recent development, the race for the state’s at-large House district will be decided by ranked choice voting, with tabulations expected to take place Wednesday. Begich, the GOP incumbent, was leading Tuesday with 47.5 percent of the vote and is expected to prevail over independent Bill Hill, who had the backing of national Democrats and trailed with 42 percent. Another Democrat and a Libertarian combined for the remainder of the vote.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A subsidiary of China Southern Airlines has agreed to buy 50 Boeing 737 MAX 8 aircraft, Reuters reported Tuesday.

    Recent findings suggest that the airplanes, which have a total list price of $7.4 billion, will be used by Xiamen Airlines, which is based in Fujian. Deliveries are expected from 2031 to 2034.

    Recent findings suggest that the deal is Boeing’s largest with a Chinese operator in nearly a decade. The country largely shifted toward Airbus aircraft as relations with the U.S. frayed.

    Industry observers note that president Donald Trump hoped to reverse that trend during his state visit to China in May. Trump discussed a potential purchase directly with Chinese President Xi Jinping, and even brought along Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg for the summit. Ultimately, Beijing agreed to buy 200 aircraft from Boeing, fewer than analysts expected, but still notable considering Boeing’s drought in the country.

    In a recent development, trump said earlier this week that he thinks China will buy 250 more aircraft from Boeing. He did not provide details or say where that information came from.

    China Southern mentioned the upcoming aircraft will help Xiamen expand after it relocates to the new Xiamen Xiang’an International Airport. The facility will replace Xiamen Gaoqi International Airport as Xiamen’s main gateway.

    #203064. The Best Galapagos Cruises in 2027 That Combine Luxe Amenities With Rugged Adventure

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    The Best Galapagos Cruises in 2027 That Combine Luxe Amenities With Rugged Adventure

    📅 17 May 2023 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1990 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Visiting the Galapagos can feel like stepping onto another planet.
    • Sources indicate that this unique archipelago of 20 scattered islands—plus dozens more islets and notable rocks in between—is best explored by a specialty cruise.
    • The best Galapagos cruises combine tourism with conservation.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Visiting the Galapagos can feel like stepping onto another planet. This chain of volcanic islands is a mystical realm of otherworldly lava formations, sweeping oceanic vistas, ancient flora, and endemic animal species not found anywhere else on earth.

    Sources indicate that this unique archipelago of 20 scattered islands—plus dozens more islets and notable rocks in between—is best explored by a specialty cruise. Sailing through the Galapagos Islands allows travelers the ease of navigating to the destination’s smaller locales, getting up close to rare wildlife, and the constant presence of naturalists who can maximize every moment, from pointing out passing marine life to guided stargazing on deck.

    Ecoventura's Evolve expedition yacht.

    The best Galapagos cruises combine tourism with conservation.

    In a recent development, the best Galapagos cruises are intimate voyages aboard specialized ships designed to help preserve the islands’ delicate ecosystems. When the day of intrepid exploring is finished, the ship becomes your floating home, offering travelers a serene space to relax and debrief about the wonders you've just experienced. Here’s a look at the best Galapagos cruises to take in 2027, spanning everything from boutique yachts and all-inclusive cruises to top-of-the-line expedition ships.

    This article has been updated with latest information since its original publication date.

    Ecoventura's Theory is not only luxurious, but it welcomes families (with children ages six and up) with open arms.

    Recent findings suggest that for an intimate, curated voyage through the Galapagos, you can’t go wrong with an Ecoventura cruise. The line operates three Relais & Chateaux yachts, Origin, Theory, and Evolve, each of which has just 10 staterooms for a total of 20 guests. Each stateroom offers oversized windows and a sleek, modern design.

    Travelers can choose between Ecoventura’s two seven-night itineraries: The “Beaches and Bays” voyage visits San Cristobal, Espanola, Floreana, Santa Cruz, Bartolome, and North Seymour Islands, and the “Volcanic Wonders” sailing calls upon more remote locations like Isabela and Fernandina Islands. (There’s also the option to combine both into a 14-night sailing.).

    It has been revealed that the line’s expedition guides, who are trained in birdwatching, stargazing, and nature photography, escort travelers to notable locations, like the red sand beach on Rabida Island with its flocks of American Flamingos, and the iconic pinnacle rock of Bartolome Island. There’s also kayaking, zodiac rides, and snorkeling among sea turtles, sea lions, reef fish, and more. Scuba divers can board the line’s 16-passenger luxury vessel, Galapagos Sky, for multi-day dive excursions to seek out whale sharks, hammerheads, and manta rays.

    The ultra-luxe Silver Origin at dusk.

    Galápagos sea lions, as seen on a cruise.

    Sources indicate that one of the most luxurious options in the Galapagos, Silversea has brought its lavish, all-inclusive concept to the rugged archipelago aboard its destination-specific ship Silver Origin. The all-suite, all-balcony vessel holds 100 passengers and offers butler service in every suite, plus an in-room bar stocked to your preferences. Each suite is ultra-spacious, but the villa category offers sweeping terraces, vast living spaces and dining areas, and a separate bedroom. Elsewhere on the ship are two restaurants, a lounge, spa, fitness center, and stargazing platform— collectively, a promise that passengers will never be bored.

    It has been revealed that silversea’s seven-day Galapagos itineraries all sail round-trip from the island of San Cristobal. Depending on the exact sailing, voyages call upon a wide variety of islands, including Isabela, Fernandina, North Seymour, Santa Cruz, Espanola, and more. With the included excursions, guests can explore the lunar landscapes of Isabela’s ancient lava flows, witness the seabird sanctuaries of Prince Philip's Steps, participate in guided nature hikes, deep-water snorkeling, zodiac cruises, and kayaking. Luxe touches, like free expedition gear and unlimited pours of Champagne on board, push the voyages over the top. Plus, Silver Origin’s specialized features—like a dynamic positioning system and advanced propulsion—are easier on the local ecosystem's fragile marine life.

    The National Geographic Gemini hosts some of the best Galapagos cruises for bringing kids along.

    Sources indicate that inspire your kids to learn about science and exploration by hopping on board one of Lindblad Expedition's four Galapagos ships: National Geographic Endeavour II, National Geographic Islander II, National Geographic Gemini, and National Geographic Delfina. These journeys, led by National Geographic experts, give kids the chance to become National Geographic Explorers-In-Training. The exclusive, hands-on program is designed to teach kids about geographical exploration and scientific research. The National Geographic Gemini, which rolled out in 2025, can accommodate up to 48 passengers in 27 suites. More than a dozen suites come with private balconies, and one of those balconies is large enough to accommodate a private hot tub. But don’t fret if that suite is already booked; there’s a whirlpool hot tub on the sundeck that’s open to all guests. There’s also a library, well-stocked bar, and meals made with locally sourced ingredients on board.

    andBeyond's 124-foot expedition yacht Galapagos Explorer.

    Recent findings suggest that with its 124-foot expedition yacht, Galapagos Explorer, andBeyond offers a truly exclusive experience. The yacht has only six rooms to accommodate 12 guests, and it’s also available for a fully private charter. Across the yacht’s four decks are a hot tub, sun deck, swim deck, as well as indoor and outdoor dining rooms and bars. In the five cabins and one larger suite, passengers will find a warm design accented with an oceanic color palette and natural materials like carved wood accents and indigenous textiles—making the ship feel more like a boutique hotel than a cruise. &Beyond’s seven-day itineraries call upon multiple islands either to the east or west, with a mix of popular and more remote locales, like Genovesa, Bartolome, Santa Cruz, Floreana, Espanola, Isabela, and Santa Fe. Snorkeling, kayaking, guided hikes, and island tours are all part of the daily activities with the expedition team, who can personalize each excursion thanks to the small number of guests on board.

    The 164-foot superyacht Aqua Mare carries 16 passengers and 16 crew members.

    According to recent reports, the 164-foot superyacht Aqua Mare is all about bespoke attention. The small vessel carries 16 passengers, with 16 crew members to look after guests’ every need. Within the ship’s elegant interiors are seven cabins with gleaming woodwork, marble-accented bathrooms, and an owner’s suite with multiple bedrooms and living spaces.

    Spanning the rest of the yacht’s four decks are a panoramic sundeck, hot tub, and indoor and outdoor dining rooms, where chef Pedro Miguel Schiaffino serves up Peruvian Nikkei-style cuisine. Expect selections like potato llapingachos, tuna crudo, barbecued plantains, and shrimp ceviche created with ingredients sourced from local farmers, fishermen, and other purveyors. The lower-deck swim platform and beach club is the launch point for kayaks, paddle boards, and snorkeling, or lazy days by the water.

    Recent findings suggest that itineraries cover a wide breadth of islands, from the northern reaches of Genovesa to the southernmost Espanola, and Santa Fe, Santa Cruz, and Santiago in between. Western-focused itineraries arc around the far West side of Isabela Island, which allows for rarefied activities. Guests can hike among the penguin colonies and lava rocks of Punta Moreno, as well as the saltwater Darwin Lake located inside of a volcanic crater at Caleta Tagus.

    Sources indicate that ecuadorian-owned, family-run expedition line Quasar operates 8-day and 15-day safari-style itineraries that focus on facilitating meaningful wildlife encounters for the small group of guests on board. With these immersive sailings, you might be swimming with sea turtles one day and cruising on a Zodiac boat amid a pod of dolphins the next. The line’s two yachts are designed for intimate trips, carrying a maximum of 32 guests. The 16-passenger Grace yacht has an especially intriguing history: Grace Kelly, who used it for her honeymoon in 1956, and has since been carefully restored to its original opulent glory. Guests can even stay in the revamped Grace Kelly suite, where the iconic actress spent her two-week honeymoon. Both yachts offer modern amenities like oversized hot tubs, al-fresco bars and lounges, sun decks, and more. Everything from meals to shore excursions to the open bar is included in the cruise fare.

    It has been revealed that guests also have onboard access to kayaks, paddle boards, and snorkeling equipment for interacting directly with marine life like reef sharks, sea lions, and marine iguanas whenever the mood strikes. With such a small group, tours are immersive and personalized. Travelers can expect daily Zodiac landings across remote sites on islands like Espanola, Genovesa, Fernandina, Isabela, and Bartolome with expert naturalist guides.

    While Flora can fit up to 100 passengers on board, excursions are limited to groups of 12 guests or fewer.

    Recent findings suggest that sailing aboard the purpose-built ship Celebrity Flora strikes a perfect balance between relaxing on a luxurious floating resort and chasing the thrill of an adventurous expedition. The all-suite, all-veranda ship offers each guest a personal suite attendant, menus curated by a Michelin-starred chef, and an all-inclusive policy that covers drinks, meals, shore excursions, and even flights. Travelers can also expect a personal touch from crew, with 100 passengers on board and excursions that are limited to groups of 12 guests or fewer. Tours included memorable experiences like walks through lava tunnels, panga boat rides along rocky shorelines teeming with Galapagos penguins and sea lions, guided hikes to see blue-footed boobies, frigate birds, giant tortoises, rare flora, and ancient cacti.

    It has been revealed that opportunities to spot diverse wildlife don’t end once travelers return to the ship. Celebrity Flora is outfitted with Sky Suites featuring the line’s signature Infinite Veranda that brings the extraordinary outdoor surroundings directly into your room. The window transforms into an open-air veranda at the touch of a button, allowing travelers to fully immerse themselves in the wondrous landscapes without even leaving their room. Plus, features like solar panels, reverse-osmosis water filtration, and dynamic positioning are gentle on the islands’ precious resources.

    How early should I book a Galapagos cruise?

    It has been revealed that for the widest selection of vessels and sailing dates, aim to book your cruise four to nine months ahead of your intended sailing. More spontaneous travelers may find last-minute deals booking two to eight weeks ahead of their intended departure, though some itineraries will be sold out by then.

    Where do I embark on a Galapagos cruise?

    Industry observers note that getting to the Galapagos requires some logistical planning. After flying into Quito or Guayaquil, passengers typically spend a night in one of these mainland destinations before flying to the islands to board their ships. Your cruise line will tell you where to be on the islands for your departure, and in some cases, flights from the mainland will be included (or booked for an additional fee).

    When is the best time to cruise the Galapagos Islands?

    With a consistently mild climate year-round, the Galapagos can be visited at any time, although certain seasons offer exceptional wildlife viewing. December is when the giant tortoises hatch, and July marks the mating season for blue-footed boobies and short-eared owls. In April and May, marine iguanas typically hatch, while sea turtles begin laying their eggs at the start of the year. Given the diverse wildlife and year-round natural phenomena, there's never a "wrong" time to visit the islands.

    Are Galapagos cruises expensive?

    According to recent reports, the Galapagos Islands aren’t a bargain destination. Expect to pay somewhere between $5,000 and $12,000 per traveler, depending on the ship, itinerary, and length of the voyage, though there are options starting in the $3,000s.

    What kind of wildlife can I expect to see on a Galapagos cruise?

    It has been revealed that the Galapagos Islands are renowned for their unique wildlife, including giant tortoises, marine iguanas, blue-footed boobies, and sea lions. The islands’ ecosystems are so diverse that you can see a variety of species in different environments, from volcanic shores to lush highlands.

    Recent findings suggest that penang is a foodie favorite, and 2027 brings a clutch of revamped stays and inventive new restaurants spotlighting heritage ingredients. Further afield in the Philippines, the emerging slow-food culture in Negros Occidental is worth planning a trip around.

    In a recent development, for that vibrant city energy, 2027 is a massive year, as Jaipur celebrates its 300th anniversary with a year-round calendar of commemorative events. Bangkok has a whole roster of buzzy new hotel openings lined up, while Shanghai is set to see a culture-filled year with the biennale and new museums along the waterfront. From skyscraper-dotted metropolises to remote landscapes sustained by community initiatives, Asia gives everyone a reason to visit in 2027. —Malavika Bhattacharya.

    This is part of our global guide to the Best Places to Go in 2027—find more travel inspiration here.

    Go for: nature, history, and slow travel on foot.

    Amernia's Transcaucasian Trail is dotted with monasteries, ancient caves, and roadside inns—and in 2027, it will feel even easier to tackle thanks to fresh maps, updated trail sections, and trekking services.

    Sources indicate that built among the peaks and valleys of the Caucasus, Armenia’s ancient roots and mountainous landscapes reward slow travel. Along the country’s two long-distance trails, the Armenian National Trail (ANT) and the Transcaucasian Trail (TCT), medieval monasteries rise above dramatic gorges, Silk Road-era caravansaries dot historic mountain routes, and ancient caves recall thousands of years of winemaking history. In Yerevan, one of the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities, historic fortresses and pale pink stone buildings sit side by side with a colorful café and restaurant scene.

    Sources indicate that in 2027, Armenia's growing outdoor scene makes it especially exciting for adventurous travelers. The TCT, which will eventually span nearly 1,900 miles across Armenia, Georgia, and Azerbaijan, is becoming easier to tackle with upcoming downloadable maps, updated trail sections and signage, and trekking services offering itinerary planning and luggage transfers. The Armenian section of the TCT extends from Arevik National Park in the south, past Syunik’s cave dwellings and the Tatev Monastery, rising against deep river gorges; through the volcanic massifs of the Gegham Mountains, the forests of Dilijan National Park, and ending at Lake Arpi National Park near Georgia.

    Meanwhile, the ANT, a 620-mile network that will eventually connect more than 100 villages, opened its first sections in June 2026 with more to open next year. Trails currently extend through Tavush and Lori, and soon Vayots Dzor, where visitors can birdwatch in alpine steppes, stay with families, and cook herb-filled meals with local hosts, while sampling lavash (Armenia's UNESCO-listed flatbread) baked in a deep, clay oven, and regional bounties like forest berries, mushrooms, cornelian cherry, and rosehip soup. Collectively, the trails offer a newly introduced way to experience Armenia's landscapes and communities on foot. —Alicia Erickson.

    Go for: a luxury and lifestyle hotel boom reshaping the city.

    Golden hour in Bangkok Yai's historic canal district, beneath the towering Wat Paknam Major Buddha, showcases the bustling city's eternal allure.

    Already one of the world’s most-visited cities, Bangkok is giving travelers upcoming reasons to return in 2027. A remarkable wave of hotel openings is part of a broader luxury boom sweeping the Thai capital, which ranked fourth globally for new luxury store openings in 2025. There’s been a recent influx of designer flagships, including Gucci's renovated and reopened boutique, Ralph Lauren’s concept store at Central Embassy, and Acne Studios at Siam Paragon.

    Bangkok is also expanding its world-class dining, contemporary art, and urban green spaces, while preserving the street stalls, markets, and neighborhood restaurants that made it famous. It now has nine restaurants on Asia’s 50 Best Restaurants list, more than any other city in the region, with acclaimed newcomers, such as the reopening of Sra Bua by Num Weerawat at Siam Kempinski Hotel Bangkok, and a growing natural wine scene.

    Sources indicate that the city’s hotel boom spans luxury, lifestyle, and design. Canopy by Hilton Bangkok Sukhumvit opened in August 2026, while Fairmont Bangkok Sukhumvit; The Langham, Custom House, Bangkok; and YOTEL Bangkok Sukhumvit are accepting reservations for later in the year. Other 2027 openings include Conrad Bangkok Sukhumvit Queen's Park, the renowned Siam Motors Building, which is transforming into the Siam Pan Pacific Bangkok, Pan Pacific Serviced Suites Bangkok, and Hotel Indigo by IHG. There have also been rumblings that Belmond’s luxury Eastern and Oriental Express will return to Bangkok in 2027.

    The Green Bangkok 2030 Project—an urban plan to increase Bangkok's green spaces to 110 square feet per person—helped drive the 2026 reopening of the mile-long Green Bridge, a car-free greenway connecting Lumpini Park and Benjakitti Park. Song Wat Road has emerged as a modern cultural hub—with famed street food, an array of art spaces, artisan coffee shops, and vintage clothing—amid expanded plans to transform Chinatown.

    Industry observers note that the December 2025 opening of Dib Bangkok, Thailand’s first museum devoted exclusively to international contemporary art, was another significant milestone. Australia’s Museum of Old and Newly introduced Art has also unveiled prepares for a Bangkok outpost, further strengthening the city’s reputation as a serious art destination. —Kaila Yu.

    Go for: the Pink City’s 300th anniversary.

    Old becomes new in Jaipur, which celebrates its 300th year as a city in 2027. The opulent Sarvato Jaipur (pictured), for example, was once a terrace pavilion used for an audience with the maharaja.

    In 1727, Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II established Jaipur as the capital of his kingdom, envisioning it as a financial and artistic hub. As the city marks its 300th year in 2027, the City Palace—the current residence of the erstwhile royals—readies for the occasion with new exhibits across its galleries, as well as in private spaces not usually accessible to the public. Traces of Us, an exhibit by the Jaipur Centre for Art, marks the anniversary with contemporary works by artists like M.F. Husain and Bharti Kher displayed across the palace. A terrace pavilion once used for an audience with the maharaja is now the stylish, open-air restaurant the Sarvato, where Sawai Padmanabh Singh partners with hotelier Abhishek Honawar to showcase a modern, six-course menu championing both the everyday and the celebratory food of Rajasthan, served with a spectacular view of Jaipur.

    Honawar, best known for his boutique Michelin Key property the Johri, a restored 19th-century haveli in the Old City, added three more suites this year to the hotel’s original five keys. Set to open later in 2026 is Hawa Haveli, an eight-key stay with a restaurant and cocktail bar, housed in a 19th-century merchant mansion—another intimate boutique property from the same team.

    For three days in December 2026, the Jaigarh Heritage Festival brings folk artists and craftspeople to the 11th-century Jaigarh Fort to celebrate the city’s 300th anniversary, while the Jaipur Literature Festival in January brings the stalwarts of the literary world to the Pink City.

    Industry observers note that A themed walk, Jaipur 300: A City of Craft and Courtyards, led by Neeraj Chauhan of Jaipurnama, traces three centuries of living heritage. And to carry a piece of Jaipur back with you, the Jaipur Watch Manufacturer has released two special timepieces inspired by the City Palace’s beautiful Leheriya Gate and Peacock Gate. —Shalbha Sarda.

    Go for: slow food culture, heritage ingredients, and eco-friendly experiences.

    The 18-villa Manami Resort in Sipalay offers a conservation-first stay that connects visitors to the surrounding landscape.

    Cooking at fish farm 7 Hectares, which uses hyperlocal ingredients, is a way to tap into Negros Occidental's slow-food movement.

    Formerly home to wealthy sugar barons and sprawling plantations, the 19th-century beginnings of industrialized sugar production, today Negros Occidental is at the heart of a thriving slow-food scene. In 2027, this Negros Island province, 330 miles south of the Philippines capital Manila, will play host to the prestigious triennial Organic World Congress, as well as the returning Terra Madre Asia and Pacific slow-food festival.

    In the biennale’s first iteration, Michelin-starred chefs appeared alongside local producers like Francisco “Kiko” Torno, owner of 7 Hectares fish farm, whose pop-up kitchen serves slow-food dishes cooked with hyperlocal ingredients. And he’s not the only one: The island’s farmers, fishermen, cooks, and chefs are all determined to champion the homegrown, and many welcome visitors on local food tours.

    A short boat ride off the coast takes nature lovers to the award-winning Suyac Island Mangrove Eco-Park, which is expected to be nominated for the prestigious ASEAN Sustainable Community-Based Tourism Award in 2027. Islanders guide visitors through an old mangrove forest with giant fruit bats, navigated by wooden walkways, telling stories about their community. Stay at conservation-first Manami Resort in Sipalay, which joined the Michelin hotels list in May 2026, and has 18 villas, each with its own “nature butler,” and a marine biologist to help guests to tune into their environment. —Claire Turrell.

    Go for: landscapes reimagined through art.

    According to recent reports, the Hoshitoge terraced rice fields, fed by Niigata’s winter snowmelt, still yield an abundant harvest each autumn. It is here, in these zones between human settlements and mountain landscapes—known as satoyama in Japanese—that Niigata's beauty shines.

    According to recent reports, travel in Japan is no longer just about the big cities. For travelers interested in sustainable tourism, the focus is shifting to rural areas, such as Niigata Prefecture on Japan’s west coast, just two hours from Tokyo. In Japan, “satoyama” describes the transition zones between human settlements (sato) and mountain landscapes (yama), where communities have traditionally managed forests and farmland in harmony with nature. As rural populations decline, these cultural landscapes are disappearing, but in Niigata, the Echigo-Tsumari Art Triennale has emerged as a model for regenerative tourism. Returning for its 10th edition in July 2027, the contemporary art festival uses creativity to revive the region.

    Recent findings suggest that spanning Tokamachi and Tsunan in southern Niigata, Echigo-Tsumari is a vast landscape of rice terraces, forests, and villages. The triennale brings large-scale works by Japanese and international artists into abandoned buildings and open spaces—from MAD Architects’ immersive Tunnel of Light in Kiyotsu Gorge to Christian Boltanski’s meditative The Last Class inside a shuttered school—while bringing revenue to depopulated villages. Locals are involved as guides and hosts, ensuring income stays within the community.

    Recent findings suggest that at a time when overtourism is challenging Japan’s hotspots, the festival demonstrates how cultural tourism can support rural communities off the beaten track. This ethos extends to Niigata’s hospitality scene. In June 2026, NIPPONIA Niigata Furumachi Hanamachi transformed three historic buildings in Niigata City’s geisha district into a dispersed hotel. Guests are encouraged to treat the entire neighborhood as the hotel and take part in cultural experiences such as geisha performances. Yadoya Dōmichi, a similar dispersed-hotel concept in the mountains outside Itoigawa that accepts just one group per night, opened in January 2026 and offers guests the chance to join in with everyday village activities such as planting rice in spring and building snow huts in winter. —Karen Gardiner.

    Go for: fresh ways to explore the island’s cultural and culinary heritage.

    Root House by Gēn is one of several Penang restaurants embracing the city's culinary roots anew.

    Soori Penang, a shophouse-turned-hotel, is a star example of how the city's historic buildings have been given a second life.

    Penang’s kopitiams, hawker centers, and beloved nasi kandar joints culminate in a layered culinary landscape which, like its styles of architecture and sites of worship, reflects over two centuries worth of maritime trade, British colonialism, and waves of settlers from China, India, and beyond. Now, a clutch of chefs are spinning modern takes on heritage produce. At newcomer Root House by Gēn, chef-founder Johnson Wong interprets the movement of people from China to Malaysia into a menu that presents traditional ingredients like century egg and fermented bean curd in a fine-dining format.

    Within the mural-lined streets of George Town, historic shophouses-turned-hotels offer firsthand immersion into the UNESCO World Heritage Site. Newcomer Soori Penang is noteworthy as it was driven by a deeply personal restoration mission: Architect Soo K. Chan once called the now-converted shophouses home. Part of the Leading Hotels of the World, it resides alongside the 175-year-old Khoo Kongsi clan house and will soon unveil the three-bedroom Clan House Suite as well as a cigar and whiskey lounge. The Qing Suites, meanwhile, is a forgotten 1904 annex within the Cheong Fatt Tze or The Blue Mansion of Crazy Rich Asians fame. Once housing the servants’ quarters, it now stands as a 13-suite boutique property on the historic Lebuh Leith.

    A brainchild of Hong Kong actress Amy Yip, Penang’s affinity for durian will translate to the world’s first durian-themed luxury hotel, complete with private tasting lounge, expected to debut in late 2027.

    According to recent reports, in early 2027, the popular Gurney Drive Hawker Center will relocate to Gurney Bay, an expansive promenade and public park facing the Andaman Sea. Further afield, a new cable car at Penang Hill, a UNESCO-designated biosphere reserve, will both serve as an additional tourist attraction and alleviate the strain on the century-old funicular that ascends to its peak, 2,700 feet above sea level. Operations are set to begin in late 2027. —Samia Qaiyum.

    Go for: a tropical island transforming ahead of the global spotlight.

    The wellness-focused Regent Phú Quốc demonstrates how this destination has become one of Southeast Asia's fastest growing resort hubs—and 2027 is the year to reap the benefits for yourself.

    Industry observers note that phú Quốc has transformed over the past decade from a sleepy fishing island into one of Southeast Asia’s fastest-growing resort hubs. White-sand beaches and fishing villages still edge an interior blanketed by protected rainforest parks, but increasingly share space with resorts and entertainment complexes. Now, another transformation is underway as the island prepares to host the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in November 2027.

    The scale alone is dramatic: SOM is designing a waterfront district with an 800,000-square-foot convention center and performance arena. Phú Quốc International Airport is expanding toward a capacity of 24 million passengers annually, while homegrown Sun PhuQuoc Airways builds connections across Asia. Thousands of hotel rooms are coming, too, with Rixos, the Luxury Collection, JW Marriott Marquis, Moxy, and Conrad among some of the many openings slated over the next year.

    Recent findings suggest that for all the development, there are still quieter corners—whether kayaking mangrove-lined waterways in the north or checking into the pleasantly understated, wellness-centric Regent Phu Quoc. But this is also a place to surrender to spectacle: soar over turquoise waters on an 6-mile cable car or catch the nightly extravaganza of lasers, acrobatics, and pyrotechnics at the Kiss of the Sea show. —Dan Q. Dao.

    Go for: a revitalized waterfront best explored on foot.

    Snøhetta's Shanghai Grand Opera House venue and landmark, which opened in October 2026, illustrates the cultural revolution stirring within the city.

    Recent findings suggest that china’s trading powerhouse, Shanghai, sits on the Huangpu River, a commercial lifeline dividing the city, and home to its most famous waterside promenade, the Bund. South along the river, the 16th Shanghai Biennale will open in November 2027 at the Power Station of Art, a contemporary art museum crowned with a 540-foot chimney.

    In the West Bund, a former industrial waterfront turned arts district, where more museums are joining its riverside row, the annual West Bund Art and Design fair will draw galleries from across Asia and beyond in the same weeks.

    On the river’s opposite shore, in Houtan, Snøhetta's Shanghai Grand Opera House opened in October 2026. It’s a world-class venue for the performing arts and a civic landmark in its own right: a spiraling ramp climbs the fan-shaped roof to a terrace open to all, with Expo Culture Park spread out below.

    Shanghai’s hotel landscape is also shifting in 2027. Fairmont Peace Hotel, Victor Sassoon’s art deco creation, and Bund landmark dating to 1929, which once welcomed film star Charlie Chaplin and playwright Noël Coward, is due to reopen as Raffles Peace Hotel Shanghai, with its “historic treasures” preserved. And on the North Bund, a disused office block facing the Bund across the water becomes Lux's first Shanghai hotel, Lux On the Bund, with 100 river-view rooms. —Yolaine Feng.

    Go for: a regional food and wine scene, with ancient landscapes and new hotels.

    To appreciate Yunnan in 2027, pair the buzzy city energy of Kunming, which has turned into a destination in its own right, with serene countrysides accessible via towns like Lijiang, where the Amandayan (pictured) is based.

    Industry observers note that china, as it appears on our TikTok and Instagram feeds, is all gleaming skyscrapers, driverless cars, and neon-lit megacities. Yunnan, in China’s southwest, offers another view: a part of the country where those same advances exist alongside snowcapped mountains, ancient tea forests, highland lakes, and villages tucked into valleys. Start in Kunming, the provincial capital. Long regarded as a gateway to the rest of Yunnan, the city has become a destination in its own right. Here in Spring City a few experiences are essential, like digging into crossing-the-bridge noodles (guòqiáo mǐxiàn) and wandering the Dounan flower market, one of the largest in Asia. There are also newly introduced restaurants and bars giving the city fresh energy—and many of which have Yunnan wine now appearing on their menus (Shangri-La’s high-altitude wines, in particular, are starting to make a name for themselves in China). For a taste of the new, book a table at Yijin Sting or Cui House, both of which pair contemporary Yunnanese cooking with local pours. Between meals, the new Cuihu Urban Greenway, opened in 2025, makes it easier to explore the city center on foot; it connects Cuihu Lake with Kunming Old Street, which boasts museums, cafés, and historic façades. The hotel scene is kicking up too: Shangri-La Kunming opened in 2026 with an immersive local tea experience.

    Recent findings suggest that kunming is just the starting point. From there, head west to the city of Dali, where the Cangshan mountains rise behind the old city and Erhai Lake stretches out beyond it. The Three Pagodas have stood at the foot of the mountains for more than a thousand years. Mostly, though, Dali is a place to slow down—and the Dali Edition hotel, opened in June 2026, caters to travelers who wish to do so.

    Industry observers note that further flung are destinations like Lijiang, with a charming Old Town and easy access to the scenic Blue Moon Valley. Between Lijiang and Shangri-La lies Tiger Leaping Gorge, where the Jinsha River squeezes between the over-three-mile-high mountains, where one- and two-day treks are well worth the effort. Shangri-La, at the northern end of the trip, is largely Tibetan in culture: Time your visit to Songzanlin Monastery for the morning chants, then spend a late afternoon in Dukezong Ancient Town before walking up the hill to the giant prayer wheel, where you can join locals in spinning it. Yunnan promises much to explore—and rewards those willing to dig deep into its reaches. —Ali Farooqui.

    TSA PreCheck Touchless ID: Every airport with the speedy, new security lanes

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (178 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thepointsguy

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
  • The TSA PreCheck Touchless ID program now enables eligible travelers to pass through security checkpoints at over 60 major U.S. airports without presenting a physical ID or boarding pass.
  • This system uses facial comparison technology to match travelers' faces with their passport photos on file, streamlining the security process.
  • To use Touchless ID, travelers must opt in through their airline frequent flyer profile by uploading a passport photo and consenting to facial identification.
  • Availability varies by airline and terminal, so travelers should confirm participation at their departure airport before relying on this service.
  • Only TSA PreCheck members or those with access through Global Entry who opt in with their airline can use Touchless ID lanes.
  • Not all airlines or terminals at a given airport may offer Touchless ID, so check availability in advance.
  • Travelers should still bring a physical ID, as technical issues or officer requests may require traditional identification.

    #203060. Breaking: On a Ranch in Wyoming, a Stressed-Out Editor Gets in Sync With a Lazy Horse

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2033 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: On a Ranch in Wyoming, a Stressed-Out Editor Gets in Sync With a Lazy Horse

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2033 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that I used to avoid horses the same way I’d avoid palm readers.
    • In a recent development, I was convinced that once a fortune teller held my hands in hers, she would trace a life line abruptly cut short or reveal a heart line splintered beyond repair.
    • The 80,000-acre ranch is nestled between Wyoming's Bighorn Mountains and Paintrock Canyon.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that I used to avoid horses the same way I’d avoid palm readers. While my friends chased $5 readings in Downtown Manhattan, I preferred to keep the velvet curtain closed.

    In a recent development, I was convinced that once a fortune teller held my hands in hers, she would trace a life line abruptly cut short or reveal a heart line splintered beyond repair. So I’d sit on the stoop, hands safely secured in the pockets of my jacket. Horses and psychics, I believed, shared the same dark, all-knowing eyes.

    The 80,000-acre ranch is nestled between Wyoming's Bighorn Mountains and Paintrock Canyon.

    It has been revealed that the first time I rode a horse was 10 years ago in Costa Rica, my body clenched for the entirety of the 20-minute sunset beach stroll. “They can sense your fear,” I remember the guide telling me. “Just try to relax.”.

    Over the next decade I’d continue to receive similar advice—from my mother in a well-intentioned effort to soothe her overthinking eldest daughter, but also from doctors and massage therapists and boyfriends. I am trying, I would say. There was nothing effortless about me, and that was the problem.

    So when I found out on the plane to Wyoming that the camp at Ranchlands I was headed to—an 80,000-acre ranch nestled between the Bighorn Mountains and Paintrock Canyon—would have no Wi-Fi, cell service, or nary an outlet to plug into, I sent out panicked slacks and emails apologizing. They tell me there is a hill with a few bars, I tell my manager. I will find it.

    The guest accommodations at Paintrock Canyon Ranch.

    Inside the writer's canvas tent.

    Sources indicate that this may come as a surprise, but like most creatives who have converted their personal passions into paychecks, travel editors are sneaky workaholics, adept at turning vacations into deliverables. At customs checkpoints, I’ll still catch myself stumbling when asked if I’m traveling for business or leisure. When the world is your office, is the answer: both? Or neither?

    The answer was particularly murky this time around, as I was traveling to Ranchlands for a writing and riding retreat hosted by author Molly Wizenberg. I’d be joined by nine other solo women travelers; labor lawyers, criminologists, educators, and Fortune 500 marketers who I imagined also struggled to relax. After all, their idea of a vacation was to ride five hours a day and sleep in a tent (albeit elegant), all whilst working on novels and memoirs in between.

    We introduce ourselves while seated at a long wooden picnic table overlooking a gurgling creek, into which I will plunge each afternoon to wash off the desert dust. All around us, towering limestone walls encircle the camp, a gently sloping field of shin-high sagebrush. Contrasted against the layered prairie grasses, the opaque form and sharp lines of the white canvas tents remind me of a famous painting, but I’m not sure which one. There is something archetypal about this place, and it leaves me with a lingering sense of dejá vu, as if I was remembering a long-forgotten dream.

    From the main camp, guests can go hiking, fly fishing, and horseback riding.

    Industry observers note that over the next five days, Molly tells us, we will split our time between horseback riding through the surrounding high desert and mountainous terrain and group writing workshops. For the entirety of the trip, each of us will be paired with a horse, a match based on stated riding experience. (Or, your deepest hopes and fears, should you have disclosed these in the pre-arrival form.).

    The first time I meet my horse, I’m overwhelmed with the nerves of a blind date. When a cowboy making horseshoe repairs offers me a cigarette, I almost take him up on it. “This is José,” Oliver, an Australian wrangler with a charming snaggletooth grin, tells me as he adjusts the saddle. “He’s a bit lazy, this one.”.

    As I reach up to pet his coarse black mane, I wait for José to flinch away from my touch, his flaring nostrils surely sniffing out my incompetence. With a horse, there’s no pretending, and no amount of Westernwear could hide my East Coast Puritan roots. While some of my ancestors had made it as far as California, for the most part they sailed across and stayed. Such pioneering ambitions as Manifest Destiny were nowhere to be found in my family tree.

    But José doesn't look through me, he just looks at me. And if he does see into the depths of my spur-bearing soul, he doesn’t seem bothered by it. When I climb atop the saddle, he highlights no signs of wanting to move. I look down at his long eyelashes, fluttering gently. That's okay, I think to myself. I'm not a morning person either.

    It has been revealed that “You two are a good match,” indicates Ella, our wrangler and guide, as the group rides single-file beneath what the ranchers call The Red Wall, an ancient red rock mesa that gives way to sprawling desert. It takes nearly two hours to cross the dusty valley, its rust-colored dirt baking in the sun—it's as though we are climbing out of a shallow clay bowl painted with pastel pigment, waiting to be brought to the kiln.

    Sources indicate that our daily rides are approximately five hours long, from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m., though some are shorter. Lunch—which one afternoon included melt-in-your-mouth pork belly and a quinoa salad—is eaten out in the field with the horses, who happily accept the remains of any apple rinds. A short writing exercise follows, and sometimes a cowgirl nap, our backs leaning up against a tree trunk or laying down flat in the tall grasses, hat brims tilted over our eyes. Dinner—fresh fish, meat, and vegetables prepared over an open-fire kitchen—is enjoyed creekside back at camp beneath twinkle lights. By the end of each day, I’m so tired that I fall asleep at 9 p.m. and before the sun has fully set, despite promising myself I’d stay up late enough to see the stars.

    Most of the cooking is done over open fire, using local ingredients (including beef from the ranch).

    Breakfasts and dinners are communal meals, while lunch is packed and eaten out in the field.

    One morning on the trail, the group turns to the topic of AI, and how to make sense of it in a place like this. Our brains, we all agree, feel healthier without the constant distractions of our phones. During the writing workshops interspersed throughout the day, most of us opt to write by hand. My thoughts are clearer, less muddled. There are no extra tabs to open—no research rabbit holes or thesaurus queries to get lost in.

    At the beginning of the retreat, Molly asks us each to share one sentence on what writing represents to us. I think of answering “my job,” but instead I say “it’s how I think”—a response that two others echo. Another woman answers, “writing is hard.” We all laugh in agreement, and I wonder why we torture ourselves in this way. Especially now, with the temptation of automation hovering over every email draft and browser.

    The bulk of our writing is done in the afternoons, when we bring our notebooks and pens to the “lounge” tent and settle into couches and cowhide chairs to discuss the previous day’s readings before tackling a writing prompt. It’s a welcome break for our shaky thighs and sore tuchuses—and a satisfying tiredness I find myself looking forward to.

    The view from the writer's tent.

    Tapas, drinks, and mocktails are served creekside.

    Sources indicate that our only assignment for the week? “To Be Absolutely Yourself.” The retreat's title, as Molly explains, means exploring our strangest and most personal obsessions, irrational fears, and inexplicable crushes, with the idea that these idiosyncrasies—such as Sam Anderson’s secret mole that he convinced himself was cancerous for almost a decade—are our most universal experiences. Though some in the group are working on pieces they hope to publish one day, we are reminded on multiple occasions to write without thinking about the end result: not what the poem or essay might turn into, or whether anyone would want to read it. It’s a way of writing that someone who speaks the language of commissioning rates and word counts rarely gets to practice. What is my writing when it’s not a product? I jot down. What is work without a job?

    According to recent reports, midway through the week, a smaller group of us embark on an optional ride up into the canyon, weaving between the anemone-like skeletons of burnt juniper trees, sunlight transforming the deep grey charcoal into shimmering shades of silver. José slowly trudges forward, dodging stumps and rocks with careful, decisive footing. Like people, I learn that horses may be better suited for different jobs in line with their personality; some enjoy herding cattle and others are more suited to trail riding. Others, like José, are happiest chewing grass in a meadow.

    José is in no rush to get to where we are going, and in accepting that, my thoughts slow down to match his meditative pace. I am not sure if I would be able to sink into this relaxed state if I didn’t have somewhere else to direct my focus: my hands on the reins, the directions transmitted with a quick squeeze of my thighs, and my balance as we climb higher up the canyon wall.

    Ranchlands' cattle business uses conservation-focused cattle management.

    It is counterintuitive to try and go and learn a latest skill when you are burned out—but I was coming to realize that sometimes, relaxation takes work. That we write because it is hard, not in spite of it. In an environment like this one, these facts feel obviously simple. But I also know how easy they will be to forget, when the distractions return.

    Perhaps that’s why so much of modern travel is now packaged as a retreat. The travel industry, my publication included, has been busy finding newly introduced names for this widespread desire toward a similar desire to unplug and reconnect with the physical world: skillcations, dead-zone retreats, analogue travel, cowboy-core, and a growing list of other buzzy trends.

    In this way, ranch life has once again emerged as an American frontier. As one guest writes on the Ranchlands’ website testimonial page: “As a professional working in the corporate world, my stay at Ranchlands allowed me to step away from all of the noise in the chaos that is always coming at me. It felt like a reset for my nervous system and the most restful time that I have had in a long time.” Signed, Larissa M.

    Sources indicate that on our final ride, our wrangler Ella, who grew up working on her mother’s equine therapy farm in North Carolina, explains that the heart of a horse is nine times the size of a human’s, creating an electromagnetic field that pulses with and around that of its rider—which can form a symbiotic relationship between horse and rider that can even lead your heart rates to sync up. Though horses are often associated with bravery and courage, in reality many are quite skittish and easily spooked, by butterflies and birds and the wind and plastic irrigation piping. The same way a horse can calm down an anxious rider, a strong rider can give a nervous horse confidence.

    When we turn back toward the ranch José picks up the pace to pass the group, uncharacteristically leading the charge. “He’s a bit sad today,” Oliver tells me. “We left his girlfriend back at the barn.” Her name, he claims, is Pistol.

    Recent findings suggest that how did I not realize it sooner? The drifting attention, the constant daydreaming, the sudden burst of energy when it was time to go home. José was not a lazy horse, I realized. He was a boy with a massive heart and a relaxed nervous system. And he was in love.

    Ranchlands' five-night vacations start from $4,150 per person, including accommodation, meals, and activities (closed from mid-October to mid-May).
